author: Sleshi Teshome Kehali
title: The Bone-Setters’ Ward: How Ancient Healers Are Filling Ethiopia’s Modern Healthcare Vacuum
content:
Reporting from Bahir Dar, Ethiopia


In a residential neighbourhood of Bahir Dar, in northwestern Ethiopia, patients visit the home of W/ro Birqe Yibre for help with injuries. Birqe, a traditional bone-setter known locally as a Wogesha, has practised for more than 20 years.


W/ro Birqe Yibre, a traditional bone-setter known locally as a Wogesha, sits in her residential courtyard in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia. She says she has practised for more than two decades. (Photo: Sleshi Teshome)


One of her patients, Yidersal Mengistu, came with a painful right foot and a bruised big toe after kicking a stone while playing football.


“I didn’t go to the hospital. To be honest, I prefer the traditional way,” Mengistu said. He explained that he had visited Birqe before for heel pain and believed her treatment had helped him. He also said she had treated him without charge on that earlier occasion.


“If I recover fully this time, I will pay her,” he said.


For Birqe, payment depends partly on what patients can afford. She said people who have money typically pay between 150 and 200 Ethiopian birr, while she treats those who cannot pay without charging them.


“If someone has no money, I treat them and tell them, ‘Go on, go home,’” she said. “You cannot turn away poor people.”


A study of 836 people with a history of injury in Mecha district, published in

BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies

, found that 46.05 per cent had used traditional bone-setting services. Social acceptance was the most commonly reported reason for seeking this care. The findings reflect the study population in Mecha district and should not be taken as a national estimate.


For patients such as Mengistu, the decision is also shaped by personal experience and trust. But the treatment of fractures and other serious injuries can carry risks when patients delay seeking medical assessment.


Knowing When to Refer


Birqe said she distinguishes between injuries she believes she can treat and those that require hospital care.


“I handle muscle pulls and minor dislocations,” she said. “If someone comes with a serious, displaced bone or a deep fracture, I tell them plainly to go to the hospital. I don’t try to touch it.”


She said she was concerned about practitioners who accept serious cases despite lacking the necessary skills to manage them.


According to Birqe, some bone-setters bind injured limbs tightly with bamboo splints, locally known as Timaq, and continue treatment even when a patient’s condition worsens. She said some eventually advise patients to seek hospital care only after several visits.


“When parents bring me a child whose hand is already ruined, I tell them: ‘Run to the hospital, I won’t touch this,’” she said.


Her account highlights a distinction within traditional practice: while Birqe says she refers serious injuries, she believes other practitioners take on cases beyond their abilities. These claims describe her experience and observations; establishing how widespread such practices are would require further evidence.


A Crooked Arm


Thomas Habtamu, a student living in Bahir Dar, said a fall during a neighbourhood football match injured his left forearm. Because of his family’s financial difficulties, he did not go to a hospital and instead sought treatment from a local Wogesha.


“The healer kept massaging it week after week, telling me to be patient,” Habtamu recalled. He said the injury was close to the joint and that the treatment did not restore the arm to its normal position.


W/ro Birqe Yibre examines the injured foot and bruised big toe of Yidersal Mengistu in Bahir Dar. Mengistu said he injured his foot after kicking a stone while playing football and chose to seek traditional treatment. (Photo: Sleshi Teshome)


“He told me that if I ever fell down and hurt the arm again in the future, he might be able to reset it then,” Habtamu said.


Habtamu has never had the arm examined at a hospital. He said his forearm remains visibly bent and that he struggles with activities such as push-ups, lifting heavy objects and prolonged gym exercise.


He contrasted his experience with that of a friend who sustained a similar injury around the same time. According to Habtamu, his friend went to hospital, underwent an operation in which a metal plate was inserted, and recovered the use of his arm within about two months.


The two accounts illustrate the different experiences the men reported. Without medical records or an examination …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Eight Years in Prison for Fighting Anti-Black Racism in Tunisia: Free Saadia Mosbah!
content:
For years, Saadia Mosbah has been one of the leading voices against anti-Black racism in Tunisia. As president of the anti-racism organisation Mnemty, she has stood up for Black Tunisians and Black migrants alike. When


violence against Black migrants escalated

 after President Kais Saied’s February 2023 statement against African migrants, she became a target of online hate campaigns.


On May 6, 2024, she was arrested. On March 19, 2026, she was sentenced to eight years in prison and a heavy fine on charges of money laundering and illicit enrichment. On June 23, the Tunis Court of Appeals upheld her conviction, along with those of five Mnemty colleagues and associates. A final appeal, filed on June 29, is now before the Court of Cassation.


Human rights movements and organisations,


including Amnesty International

, have denounced the irregularities in the proceedings and the lack of evidence for the alleged offences. They have also raised the alarm over the racist treatment and violence Saadia has reportedly suffered in detention.


Saadia’s case sits within a wider pattern of repression. Since President Kais Saied seized sweeping powers in July 2021, Tunisia has slid back into authoritarian rule. Since May 2024, the month of Saadia’s arrest, the authorities have waged

a systematic crackdown on civil society

: activists prosecuted, organisations suspended, independent voices jailed. Throughout, the European Union has kept its

2023 migration deal with Tunisia

 in place, funding the country to stop people crossing to Europe and outsourcing its borders to a government that imprisons those who defend Black migrants. In this climate of repression and European complicity, Saadia’s voice and her freedom matter more than ever.


Saadia is more than a case file. Below, three activists tell their stories of the woman they know and the movement she helped build. Read them, then join the call for her immediate and unconditional release and for the convictions to be overturned. Keep fighting for those who fight for us in an anti-Black world.


 


Saadia’s Imprisonment Inseparable from Criminalisation of Black Organising and Solidarity


I first met Saadia Mosbah shortly after the 2011 Tunisian Revolution, when she was active in feminist organisations. Over the years that followed, I witnessed her unwavering commitment to the struggle for Black dignity, justice, and liberation in Tunisia. I watched her organisation, Mnemty, grow. And I watched a dream grow alongside it: the dream of a Tunisia where racism would no longer be denied, normalised, or left unpunished. 


A Tunisia with a law explicitly criminalising racial discrimination. Saadia was determined to bring together as many voices as possible around this struggle. She openly confronted a reality that many preferred to ignore: a significant part of Tunisia’s supposedly progressive and activist civil society remained silent on racism. Even within movements claiming to fight for equality and justice, Black people were too often expected to fight their battles alone.


Saadia refused that silence. She refused to make racism a secondary issue, or to soften her political demands to make others more comfortable.


But through years of persistence, political courage, and collective organising, she helped build a movement strong enough to achieve a historic victory: the adoption of Tunisia’s law against racial discrimination in 2018.


Years later, in 2023, I had the privilege and honour of working alongside Saadia to organise a march against state racism. Following the Tunisian presidency’s disgraceful statement targeting sub-Saharan African migrants, she was there, standing with us on the anti-fascist front line, organising, mobilising, supporting, and defending Black people and migrants in Tunisia. Saadia knew the risks. She understood what it meant to confront state racism in an increasingly authoritarian political climate. Yet she refused to retreat.


Today, Saadia est en prison. Her imprisonment is inseparable from the criminalisation of Black political organising, anti-racist resistance, and solidarity with migrants.


Saadia’s story is also a reminder that political victories are never irreversible.


A law can be adopted while the structures of domination it was meant to challenge remain intact. Rights written into legislation mean little when those who fought for them are deprived of their freedom.


But Saadia’s struggle is bigger than her imprisonment. It …

author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.


Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.


After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.


The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.


The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.


The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.


At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.


“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.


The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.


Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.

Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure

author: Tsogo Kupa
title: The country that never grieved
content:
It is said that the best films are those that truly begin only once they’re over. When the film’s images are embedded in your memory, its noises echo in your ears, and its themes steep in your thoughts. This is not to say the viewing experience itself isn’t transformative, but when films reach for something higher than distraction and pure entertainment, they offer something you take home with you, a meditation. 

Advik Beni’s feature debut,

Mother, you have not died yet. But you will. And when you do, you will finally be alive again

, is one of those meditations, and it’s rooted in mourning: for a mother, a country, a city, and an identity. It’s teeming with texture, pictured in warm, cotton-pulpy celluloid, and elevated by a sound design that balances the granular and mosaic. It blurs the lines between fact and fiction, and while there are moments that too obviously remind you that you’re not watching a documentary, its grounding in the factual gives the film a unique brilliance.

The film’s simple plot, of a middle-aged woman in Cato Manor taking care of her ailing mother, betrays the contours of memory, culture, family, and history the film traverses.

Mother, you have not died


yet

 is an experimental documentary that makes the political personal. Similar to Milisuthando Bongela’s acclaimed self-titled film, it rummages through personal and family archives to explore the sinews of what South Africa means to South Africans in the many iterations of what it has been. It centers its personal and historical inquiry around the reverberating question of what it means to be Indian in post-apartheid South Africa. 

It’s not the first film to explore South African Indian identity, but it’s the first I’ve seen that attempts to reconcile the beauty, grief, and conflicts that form part of Indian identity in South Africa. The country’s first Indians came as indentured laborers in the 19th century to service the growing sugar plantations in KwaZulu-Natal. The ethno-national group wove its own identity into the tapestry of South Africa’s growing industrialized cultural landscape; yet its relationship with Black South Africans has been tumultuous. Many of these frictions and wounds merge in Cato Manor, a neighborhood in the port city of Durban originally inhabited by former Indian indentured laborers. Appropriately, Cato Manor is where

Mother, you have not died

 yet, takes place. The city bears the weight of historical racial violence between Blacks and Indians, and the preservation and decay of its first inhabitants’ heritage. 

I talked to the writer & director of the film, Advik Beni, a South African filmmaker, programmer, and teacher based in Los Angeles. In the interview, we try to peel back the layers of their ambitious feature debut and put its kaleidoscope of ideas into focus.

Mother, you have not died yet

 had its world premiere at the FID Marseille film festival this year, where it won the Audience Award and recently celebrated its North American debut at the Camden International Film Festival.

Tsogo Kupa

I can see overtures between your work and Milisuthando Bongela’s. Why do you think this experimental and auto-ethnographic form of storytelling has been useful when trying to navigate what it means to live in a post-apartheid South Africa?

Advik Beni

It’s like at the forefront of every work I make. So our industry is so new, but we find a lot of the films falling into a sort of European, Western model of filmmaking. And it’s not just a South African issue. A lot of countries that have gone through this history of colonialism adapt to that Western model of storytelling. But for me, one of the beautiful things about being South African is our type of storytelling, our oral traditions. And this goes cross-culturally. So that’s something I always try to adapt into cinema, which is like an impossible task. As soon as you write or record orality, it’s not orality anymore. It loses the beauty of it, which is that mutability, that ability to change and adapt and go in with humor, or pull away the humor from an audience. You can’t really do that in cinema. But I think it’s something, as South African filmmakers, we should be trying to do, which is to find our own language and our own form of filmmaking. And for me, it’s fallen between this world of experimental essay, ethnographic, and the personal, because I think, like all countries, but more so in South Africa, the personal is inseparable from the …

author: APTN National News
title: Chiefs in Ontario call for province to cancel proposed law Bill 140
content:
The

Chiefs of Ontario

 says it’s calling on the province to withdraw a proposed law it says will “weaken environmental protections, reduce transparency, and undermine First Nations’” rights.


The Building Ontario Faster Act

(Bill 140)

 was introduced Oct. 27 and includes several sections that will change a number of laws in the province.


Considered an “omnibus bill,” the proposed law will amend several laws currently on the books dealing with animal health, highways, heritage, public transportation and the province’s energy board.


The chiefs say the bill is going to affect their “ability to meaningfully participate in decisions affecting their lands, rights, and communities.”


“Following the passage of Bill 5, the Protect Ontario by Unleashing Our Economy Act, 2025, Bill 140 represents another attempt by Premier Doug Ford’s government to fast-track development at the expense of critical environmental protections and First Nations rights,” said the statement.


The proposed bill is also promising to make “significant changes” to the Environmental Assessment Act, Environmental Bill of Rights, Ontario Heritage Act, and Planning Act.


“These changes would reduce environmental review requirements, limit opportunities to challenge government decisions, and weaken existing protections for First Nations lands and cultural heritage,” said the chiefs.


According to Grand Chief Joel Abram of the Association of Iroquois and Allied Indians, “When governments remove environmental protections and limit opportunities for First Nations to participate, they create greater uncertainty for everyone involved.”


“Projects move forward successfully when First Nations are treated as partners, not obstacles. Bill 140 should be withdrawn, and Ontario must work with First Nations to develop a better approach.”


One of the issues the

chiefs

 have is that the proposed law will remove the need for an environmental assessment for the Build Highway 69 Faster Act. Hwy 69 runs 140 km from Perry Sound to Sudbury.


According to the text of Bill 140, the law would require  minister of Transportation to prepare an “Indigenous consultation plan, a draft environmental study report and a final environmental study report for the Project.”


Read More: 


Carney and Ford sign deal to speed up environmental approvals while First Nations fight back in court 


According to Abrams, proposed changes to the Heritage Act will “allow individuals other than licensed archaeologists to undertake sensitive archaeological work.”


“The proposed framework would also rely on proponents attesting to their own compliance with provincial requirements, without comprehensive, mandatory First Nations consultation,” he said. “These changes put burial grounds, sacred sites, ancestral remains, and cultural heritage at risk of irreversible damage. Once these sites are disturbed or destroyed, that harm cannot be undone.”


Bill 140 is currently in second reading in the province’s legislature.


The federal government has introduced similar legislation to support the fast tracking of infrastructure projects across the country. Bill C-39 is currently being studied by special committees in the House of Commons and the Senate.

Chiefs in Ontario call for province to cancel proposed law Bill 140

 appeared first on

APTN News

.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Gull-Masty, Obed to announce new approach to support Inuit children
content:
Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty and Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami president Natan Obed are set to announce “a new approach to supporting Inuit children,” according to a media advisory from the minister’s department.


The announcement is scheduled for 10:45 a.m. Wednesday at the National Press Theatre in Ottawa.


It will follow a $575-million, five-year funding commitment for the Inuit Child First Initiative in Budget 2026, which was $25 million short of the $600 million ITK requested in its pre-budget submission.


The funding will support the transition to Pirutsiagutiit, a new program that was developed with ITK and the four Inuit treaty organizations.


The program, expected to launch Apr. 1, 2027,

will transfer responsibilities from Indigenous Services Canada to the treaty organizations or their designates.


The Inuit Child First Initiative provides health, social, educational and other supports to Inuit children and youth. Launched in September 2018, it operates alongside Jordan’s Principle, which provides similar supports to First Nations children.


The program’s future had been uncertain as its funding approached its scheduled end in March 2025. Ottawa extended funding through a one-year commitment while it worked on a replacement.


In November 2025, Gull-Masty told Nunatsiaq News the initiative would be retooled and made permanent but did not provide a timeline.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Mullin Took Government Plane to Football Game Amid Mass Flight Cancellations
content:
The DHS secretary defended the trip, in which he attended the game in a box with a major DHS contractor.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

As thousands upon thousands of travelers cancelled plans or were stranded at the airport due to the lingering effects of the ground stop on Saturday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin took a trip on a government jet to Louisiana to attend a college football game in a private box with a major contractor for his agency.

The New York Post first reported on Tuesday that Mullin took a government plane to attend the Louisiana State University (LSU) home game against University of Texas on Saturday. This was just a day after the Trump administration issued an hours-long nationwide ground stop that affected an estimated 1.5 million travellers, with over 9,200 flights cancelled.

Though Mullin made it to the game, issues for regular travelers persisted on Saturday. Data shows that nearly 6,700 flights on Saturday were cancelled, and over 9,100 delayed, according to FlightAware.

Once at the game, the Post reported, Mullin was hosted in the private box of Ben Bordelon, a major GOP donor and CEO for Louisiana-based Bollinger Shipyards. The company is a major Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contractor; just in July, the department announced it had awarded Bollinger Shipyards with a $2.2 billion contract to construct polar icebreakers for the Coast Guard.

Mullin seemingly confirmed the reporting in an interview with CNBC on Tuesday in which he defended his trip.

He said that he’s required to fly in a government plane and would have “never went if the … airways weren’t completely open, they’[d] been completely open for 21 hours,” even though the ground stop was still having effects at the time, and its cause is still being investigated.

“We’ve still gotta live life, at the same time, we’ve still got family, friends, but we also have work we do every day,” Mullin said.

He also tried to defend the box seats with Bordelon, saying that it was House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana) who arranged the tickets for him. OpenSecrets shows that Bordelon has given tens of thousands of dollars to Scalise’s PAC in recent years, as well as numerous other GOP fundraising groups.

“There was never a connection, or never business spoke[n] about that while I was there,” he said of Bordelon. “And like I said, Steve Scalise was who helped me get the tickets.”

The DHS secretary said that he has to pay the government back for the travel and will also pay “fair market value” for the box seats, though it’s unclear to whom those payments would be given.

Mullin’s trip is just one of numerous flight-related scandals in the Trump administration. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was also recently reported to be using a government jet on a regular basis to attend football games at the University of Florida, as well as for personal trips, with a large security apparatus there to accompany him. The Washington Post noted in that report that officials do reimburse the government for the travel, but at a fraction of the actual cost.

Earlier this year, the Post also reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was using a military jet for trips around the country as he was doing campaign stops for Republican midterm candidates.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $23,000 in the next 48 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Valerie Anne
title: LGBTQ+ Representation in Television Hits Devastating Lows
content:
As I’m sure you’ve noticed, LGBTQ+ representation in media is at the lowest it’s been in over a decade.

GLAAD’s latest Where We Are in TV study showed some bleak results that reflect the state of the country due to the hateful administration we live under and the wealthy conservatives who own most of the media conglomerates. Trans representation took the biggest hit, going from 33 characters to a measly SEVEN, and since three of them were on shows that were cancelled and four are from limited series, none of those seven will be returning next season. NONE. Devastating.

Twenty-five percent of LGBTQ+ characters have left our screens since last year, which brings the stats to their lowest point in over a decade. Cable television hit a 16-year low. BLEAK.

Streamers have more queer representation than cable and broadcast characters put together, but we have lost almost 100 characters from streamers as well, so even that isn’t great news. And combining streaming, cable, and broadcast, of all LGBTQ+ characters, 44% of them are characters of color, which is the lowest percentage since GLAAD’s 2017-2018 report.

Pride points out that it seems wild to imagine because some of the buzziest shows of the last few years feature queer characters: The Hunting Wives, Hazbin Hotel, Pluribus, Stranger Things, Heated Rivalry. I don’t think this show made it into the count, but we also have Sterling Point and now The Body. Queer people show up for shows that feature them, and queer people are great at telling unique stories. Alas, too many higher-ups lean on outdated Christian ideals and won’t invest in us in an effort to silence us.

This is especially wild because, while it reflects what the political times want you to believe (that queer people are outsiders, among other things), it doesn’t reflect the actual statistics. Every generation reports identifying as gayer than the last, so representation should also be at a steady increase to reflect reality, not a drastic decrease.

The actual numbers of LGBTQ+ characters on broadcast and cable shows are harrowing to look at. There are dozens of characters on any given TV show, and dozens of shows on each network, and yet the highest number among them is HBO with 15 characters. The second-highest is a big drop down, with Fox and Starz coming in with 10 characters each.

The numbers start off a little more promising for streaming, with 116 on Netflix, but then they also start dropping dramatically, with 68 on Prime Video and then again a steep drop to Hulu with 24.

I’m sure you, like I have, felt the shift even before you saw these numbers. Here at Autostraddle, we used to have to have a weekly TV roundup because there were so many queer characters on cable and broadcast shows that we couldn’t keep up with individual recaps. We used to do Pop Culture Fix twice a week to keep up with the news coming at us from all angles. And now there aren’t enough recurring characters for a weekly roundup and barely enough news for 10-15 links a week in a pop culture roundup.

It’s disheartening to see these numbers go down more and more every year when we were in such a steady incline for so long, but the fact is: We’re still here. We’re still out here writing well-rounded characters and telling our stories and watching and supporting the LGBTQ+ characters we DO still have on TV. We will not go quietly into the night. We will keep shouting and keep showing up for the queer shows doing it right until these numbers make sense again.

author: Gaurav Kumar
title: How India’s Cockroach movement maintains nonviolent discipline
content:
This article

How India’s Cockroach movement maintains nonviolent discipline

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


On Nov. 7, the eve of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, the leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, including founder Abhijeet Dipke, were not at home. They were marching in Kochi, a port city in the southern state of Kerala, nearly 1,300 miles from Delhi. 


The march echoed the two demands the movement had been shouting in Delhi’s streets since the first week of October: Scrap the nationwide recheck of voter rolls that began in June 2025, and sack the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. 


The Cockroach movement came into being in May of this year and won its first victory in July, pushing India’s education minister out of office over a leaked national medical entrance exam. The open question then was whether

a movement with no one leader and no office

 would still be around after winning its first fight. It is, and while it still has no office, it has picked a much bigger fight. Not an exam this time, but the vote itself.


The Election Commission, which runs India’s elections, is rechecking every one of India’s nearly one billion voters. In the name of clearing the rolls of the dead, the duplicated, people who have moved and what its

June 2025 order

 called “foreign illegal immigrants,” it has

purged more than 130 million

 voters. In Delhi alone, the cleanup has knocked 4.76 million people, nearly a third of the city’s electorate, off the voter list. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, strongly backs the recheck, saying that it’s necessary to strike undocumented migrants from neighboring Bangladesh, particularly Muslims, who have slipped onto the rolls. Amit Shah, Modi’s home minister and most powerful lieutenant, has defended the recheck as a way to “detect, delete, deport” what he calls infiltrators.

But critics charge

 that the rolls are being manipulated to benefit the BJP. They say the recheck shifts the burden of proof onto voters, and that the people least likely to have the required documents are the ones being dropped. 


Human Rights Watch found

 that the purge has disproportionately affected women, the poor and Muslims; in one area of West Bengal that is nine percent Muslim, more than 92 percent of those deleted were Muslim.

Opposition leaders

 have called the recheck a backdoor version of the National Register of Citizens, a citizenship list the BJP promised in 2019 to extend across India.


Presiding over it all is Kumar, whose commission both referees India’s elections and runs the recheck. He was handpicked by Modi in February 2025 under a new law giving Modi more power over the selection, in a decision announced late at night over the written dissent of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi.


In late September, the national daily

The Indian Express


reported

 that two of the election commission’s three members, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had objected on record at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions and orders tied to the recheck that they say were issued in the commission’s name without their knowledge. (In an official statement, the commission maintained that all of its decisions on the recheck were unanimous.) 


Previous Coverage


What India’s Cockroach Party won — and what’s next


The Cockroach movement, which had been pressuring the government since July over broken promises, responded by calling Kumar the biggest threat to India’s democracy and giving him 48 hours to resign.


When Kumar ignored the movement’s deadline, it took to the streets of Delhi and other cities on Oct. 2, the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, who led India’s nonviolent struggle for independence.


Unlike most Indian police forces, Delhi’s police do not answer to the city’s elected government but to the federal Home Ministry, run by Shah. It answered the protests the way it did in July, only harder. On Oct. 10 police detained more than 2,000 people in Delhi, opposition leaders and journalists among them, while about 600 were detained in Mumbai, India’s financial capital, and mobile internet went dark in the heart of Delhi.


Two days later

, Jantar Mantar — a square just a short walk from Parliament that has been Delhi’s main protest site for decades and was occupied by the movement for five weeks this summer — was …

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Administration’s Bid to Restrict Gender Affirming Care for Incarcerated People
content:
On October 21, 2026, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request to restrict medical treatment and accommodations for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision allows a lower court order blocking the policy to remain in place while the legal challenge proceeds. The ruling is an important development in the ongoing debate over transgender rights, access to healthcare, and the federal government’s authority over incarcerated people.

The dispute began after President Donald Trump issued an executive order restricting federal funding for certain medical treatments for transgender people in government custody. In response, the Bureau of Prisons introduced a policy that would end hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries for incarcerated people with gender dysphoria. The policy also sought to restrict certain accommodations for transgender prisoners.

Gender dysphoria is the distress some people experience when their gender identity does not align with their sex assigned at birth. The administration argued that these gender-affirming treatments were not necessary and that restricting them was justified by security and administrative concerns within federal prisons.

However, the policy faced legal challenges from three transgender people incarcerated in federal prisons, including one transgender woman and two transgender men. Their attorneys argued that the new restrictions would force the end of treatments that the Bureau of Prisons had provided to people with gender dysphoria since 1992.

The policy could affect nearly 1,000 incarcerated people in federal custody. The lawsuit raises questions about whether the government can discontinue established medical treatments for incarcerated people and what constitutional protections apply to people in its custody.

A lower federal court blocked the administration from enforcing the policy. The Justice Department then appealed to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to pause that ruling and allow the restrictions to take effect while the case continued. On October 21, the Supreme Court rejected the emergency request in an unsigned order. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas stated that they would have granted the request. The decision leaves the lower court’s order in place, preventing the administration from immediately enforcing the restrictions.

However, the Supreme Court’s decision does not resolve the underlying lawsuit or determine whether the administration’s policy is constitutional. The legal challenge will continue in the lower courts.

The case highlights the challenges transgender people face when seeking health care in settings where the government controls their medical decisions. Incarcerated people depend on prison authorities for access to doctors, medication, and other necessary services so when a policy restricts particular treatment, people in custody may have limited options for obtaining care independently.

Although the ruling does not end the case, it prevents the Trump administration from immediately implementing the restrictions while the legal proceedings continue. The outcome of the lawsuit will have important consequences for transgender people in federal prisons if the restrictions are placed and as the case moves forward, it shows the importance of questioning how government policies affect vulnerable populations and how government decisions apply to people whose freedom and access to healthcare are already limited.

author: kelsie kilawna
title: The taste we’ve been missing
content:
Graphic by Lauren Marchand


The clanking of pots and pans and the ringing of laughter while moving around the kitchen were always calming sounds to me growing up. 


The most important lessons I’ve learned about food came as I stood at the hips of my grandmothers, watching them peel potatoes and listening to their stories.


I am a culinary storyteller of syilx foodways. In my work at

Smoke on the Plateau

, I teach through food. I share stories about my syilx/Okanagan homelands through a fully embodied experience bringing together taste, sight, smell and sound. My research has been lifelong and has taken place in kitchens, in berry patches, and while waiting for salmon and deer to return so I could help prepare it for the people. 


There is a beauty to this way of knowing and living, because it is what taught me to be slow and patient with the offerings of our land.


The work I do honours the relationships that collapse time and place into story. It is a way of ensuring we never forget the importance of our Four Food Chiefs system. In essence, this is a reaffirmation of our governance system. 


Now, today when you enter the Okanagan Valley, you see another food story being told. A palate cleanser for the gentrification of our foodways.


What’s missing from culinary discussions


A rising culinary hotspot, the Okanagan has dressed itself in words like “local,” “seasonal,” “farm-to-table.” While wine glasses clink and tasting notes are murmured, words like “terroir” roll off the tongue as a somewhat promise to its authenticity.

It is a beautiful and comfortable story.


Terroir is a French term embraced by the culinary industry to speak to “the taste of place.” The concept itself describes how the climate and land conditions of an area affect the flavour profile of local food crops. 


In the Okanagan this is popularized through the wine industry. It’s often the terroir of a wine that is showcased through wine tastings. It speaks to the soil, weather, topography and tradition that shape what consumers taste. 


“Local” has now become a premium label, “farm-to-table” has become marketing copy, and “terroir” has become a way to charge more for the same soil that syilx Peoples have been tending since the time of our Creation, without acknowledging who did the tending, or what was given back in return.


This is gentrification. 


Not just through the extractive wine industry, but it’s become the gentrification of taste itself. 


When terroir is extracted from its French roots and planted in the Okanagan, it lands on soil that is already alive with syilx knowledge and responsibility. 


First Foods Board, Smoke on the Plateau Catering, An assortment of homesmoked deer and elk sausages, cedar smoked candied salmon, accompanied by homemade xusem raspberry compote, and siya jam. Photo by kelsie marchand (kilawna)


As a syilx culinary storyteller, I am responsible for reminding people of this, that our foodways should not be minimized for the sake of an entertaining evening.


Our foodways have and always will be prayed over. Ceremonies of health, and gratitude are held for all our homelands offer us. Young people go through their Coming of Age ceremony learning to pray for the health of our waterways. All of this is the missing spirit of the term terroir.


So I’ve been working to name what’s missing. One word, something that can hold the weight of kinship, of reciprocity, of generations coiled into one. Something that reminds us we are part of the land, not separate from it.


So I call it by it’s name, tmixʷ.


tmixʷ is the nsyilxcen word for life-force, the aliveness of every being that makes a place what it is, it speaks far beyond just soil and climate. Rather it speaks to the kinships between all of it, our reciprocity, and our syilx/Okanagan obligation to give back, so that what you take can live again.


The syilx/Okanagan understanding of place is through tmxʷulaxʷ, which speaks to the life-force-place. It is a dynamic, regenerative relationship between all beings, which the culinary industry’s shallow “local” label cannot contain.


The Okanagan culinary industry wants you to taste place, so what they’re selling is terroir, but what its missing is tmixʷ.


What tmixʷ tastes like


Let me tell you a story about xusem (soapberries).


There’s a small spot in the Okanagan mountains that has the sweetest soapberries my family has ever tasted. 


The oldest person in my family shared that those berries are …

author: David S. D'Amato
title: La Via Libertaria all’egalitarismo
content:
Di

David S. D’amato

. Originale:

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

, del 14 novembre 2014. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Secondo uno

studio recente di Emmanuel Saez e Gabriel Zucman per l’Ufficio nazionale per la ricerca economica

, “

lo 0,1% delle famiglie [americane] possiede tanta ricchezza quanto il 90% meno ricco

”. Sempre secondo lo studio, la tanto declamata “ripresa” non ha raggiunto la classe media; i benefici sono andati alla cima della piramide.


Mentre una piccola frazione della popolazione ammassa gran parte della ricchezza nazionale, esperti e accademici accusano e offrono soluzioni. Com’è facile immaginare, si accusa il libero mercato di causare differenze crescenti di ricchezza e reddito. Fautori delle liberalizzazioni e del libero mercato, i libertari sono spesso accusati di vivere in un mondo di fantasia, di ignorare il problema della disuguaglianza.


Siamo noi stessi a farlo: quando si arriva al dunque, troppi si sentono a disagio, si difendono sostenendo che la disuguaglianza

non è

 un problema, e che bisogna invece vedere lo stile di vita o qualche altro parametro. “Il capitalismo è un bene per i poveri!” Invece i libertari dovrebbero accettare il semplice fatto che la disuguaglianza è un grosso problema.


Non dobbiamo vedere nella disuguaglianza un punto debole del discorso sulla libertà economica, o una questione irrisolvibile. Le attuali relazioni economiche non sono il risultato della libertà di scambio o della legittima proprietà privata. In fatto di disuguaglianza, la ragione sta dalla parte dei libertari. Libertà e eguaglianza sono di fatto complementari, si rafforzano reciprocamente: dalla prima deriva la seconda.


Anarchici individualisti come Lysander Spooner sostenevano che “ricchezza e povertà estreme” sono il risultato del “diritto positivo”, sostituiscono il diritto naturale con un diritto arbitrario, “danno vita a monopoli e privilegi”. Sotto il capitalismo, spiega, chi possiede un certo capitale ha un particolare potere economico che non ha niente a che vedere con la libertà di produrre, scambiare e competere. In un’ottica generale, l’intervento dello stato beneficia chi è ricco e ha appoggi politici, oltre alle élite che possono influire su chi scrive e applica le regole che tutti dobbiamo rispettare.


Il meccanismo non è perfetto, e per questo sopra il capitalismo monopolistico troviamo tutto uno strato di misure chiaramente intese a proteggere i lavoratori, i consumatori e i poveri. Ma nessuna di queste misure riesce a intaccare l’obiettivo di fondo dell’intervento statale, il quale espropria i legittimi proprietari e mette le masse al servizio dei datori di lavoro. L’obiettivo storico dello stato, in breve, è la lotta di classe permanente, l’uso del proprio potere per tenere al sicuro un’aristocrazia socioeconomica.


La sinistra istituzionale ha certamente ragione sull’uguaglianza, ma tende a sbagliare in fatto di libertà, diritti individuali e mercato. L’anarchismo di mercato è per la libertà

ma anche

 per l’uguaglianza, e vuole una società senza stato in cui la legge ultima sia la parità di libertà e autorità.


La vera competizione aperta è una forza che ha il potere di dissolvere e disperdere. I libertari dovrebbero smettere di giustificare le attuali sconcertanti disuguaglianze come se fossero il risultato del

laissez-faire

 e della sovranità individuale.


Le nostre traduzioni sono finanziate interamente da donazioni. Se vi piace quello che scriviamo, siete invitati a contribuire. Trovate le istruzioni su come fare nella pagina

Sostieni C4SS

:

https://c4ss.org/sostieni-c4ss

.

title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

 serves as a blueprint for renewed efforts to confront imperial and capitalist violence as anarchist militants living at the nexus of US empire and global capital .


Email:

 nyc@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:

 @blackrose_nyc


Are you organizing at your workplace, on your campus, or in your neighborhood? Looking for a political home in which you can strategize with others about how to build power, force concessions, and push our mass movements in a revolutionary direction?


Black Rose/Rosa Negra could be right for you.


Read our

Join

 page and send us a membership inquiry!

Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago

author: Victoria Valenzuela
title: Incarcerated Los Angeles Youth Fought for the Right to Hug Their Parents — and Won
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Mercedes Maradiaga sat across from her 19-year-old son in the Los Padrinos Juvenile Hall in Los Angeles in complete devastation. Her son had at that point been incarcerated at the prison for two years and she had visited him every weekend. But that day in September 2024 was especially hard because it was their first visit since he had been beaten by officers earlier that week in a space in the jail where there were no cameras. The guards had jumped on and kicked him, and he needed surgery for a torn ACL. All she wanted was to give him a hug and reassure him that she was there. However, because of the no-contact visit policies at Los Padrinos, she was unable to give him that comfort.


Even during birthdays and holidays, they weren’t allowed to embrace. The boy endured the jail’s horrible living conditions — including rat infestations and flooded toilets — but couldn’t hug his mom for a moment of escape.


“I couldn’t even let him know I’m here just with the little hug,” Maradiaga said. “It would have meant everything to him. It was sad, and I did that for four years.”


Los Padrinos had

reopened a year earlier

 in 2023, after being shut down in 2019 due to conditions that violated the Board of State and Community Corrections (BSCC) standards, including abuses by staff. Six officers were criminally charged with

assault and child abuse

 for using pepper spray on several teenage girls. Reports

also cited a decreasing youth population

 as a factor for closure, yet staff

claimed to feel “outnumbered.”

 When Los Padrinos closed, youth were shuffled to another facility called Central Juvenile Hall — and then in 2023, that facility was closed down due to similar issues. Los Padrinos reopened, and just months later, the abuses restarted. In 2025,

30 officers were criminally charged

 by the California Attorney General with child endangerment and abuse, conspiracy, and battery for encouraging “gladiator fights” that pit youth against each other.


Olivia Shields, a justice transformation policy coordinator at Urban Peace Institute, described the constant closing and reopening of BSCC facilities as a “cycle of noncompliance.” Shields said the Los Angeles County Probation Department has ultimately failed with these maneuvers to address the core issue: unmet youth needs — which won’t be addressed through incarceration but through coordinated care in the form of individualized, robust support systems and resources.


“Rather than decarcerate these populations of young people and find community-based alternatives or step-downs for as many of them as possible, they basically shift the youth around from facility to facility to avoid noncompliance,” Shields said.


Long before the closing of Los Padrinos in 2019, the facility had a bad reputation among Angelenos. Maradiaga recalled hearing disturbing stories about the facility in the ’80s when she was a kid.


“I think it needs to be shut down,” Maradiaga said. “I think that there needs to be a better way for the youth. I don’t think locking them away from their family is the answer.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


Barred From Basic Human Contact


When Ilana Parach, executive director and co-founder of

Hoops 4 Justice

, went inside Los Padrinos with a basketball and mentorship program, she quickly learned about what youth were facing inside. She felt it was important to give them a platform to express their needs directly, so she pivoted to working with them on legislation.


“They made a list of specific programs they wanted — resources for their families, reentry support,” Parach said. “At the bottom of that list, they wrote, ‘We want to hug our moms.’”


Incarcerated youth directly told her that one parent who hugged her son during a visit on his birthday then had her visit terminated and future visits suspended for two weeks. She said another youth was incarcerated for three years and had no choice but to watch his mother cry during the visits because she couldn’t hug him.


Contact visitation policies vary across California and are often left at the discretion of correctional officers. Parach said youth and staff both told her that Los Padrinos stopped allowing contact visits after the pandemic. Parach said that during meetings of the board of supervisors, she heard officers citing staffing shortages …

author: The Canadian Press
title: Mohawk teacher, 73, earns McGill’s first PhD in Indigenous Language Revitalization
content:
By her own estimate, Mary Onwá:ri Tekahawákhwen McDonald has taught the Mohawk language to thousands of students over the past decades, from elementary school all the way to university level.


But when someone suggested she might pursue a PhD, the idea of returning to class in her 70s was a daunting prospect.


“(I said) ‘no, why would I want to do that?'” the now-73-year-old says with a laugh. ” … How do I compete with 20-year-olds? Can I really do this?”


Today, the Mohawk educator, linguist and elder can add the title of “doctor” to her list of accomplishments. Earlier this year, she became the first person to graduate from McGill University with a PhD in Indigenous Language Revitalization.


McDonald said she was eventually convinced to apply to the program out of a desire to write down the knowledge she’s accumulated over 45 years of teaching and studying language.


McDonald, who is from the Akwesasne community that straddles Quebec, Ontario and New York, is a native Mohawk speaker who only learned to speak English in second grade.


She went on to study Iroquoian linguistics, with a concentration in Mohawk, in university in Albany, N.Y., and later got a teaching certification in Ontario.


Over the years, she said, she became interested in studying how native speakers learn the language as children.


“Kinship words” used to describe close relatives come first, she said, followed by the words used to describe other people close to them. Pronouns, commands, and nouns follow, as children learn increasingly complex sentences.


She said she learned that this knowledge can help to teach second-language students, too. “If you follow this pattern, you’re coming very close to duplicating a natural learning pattern,” she said.


McDonald summed up part of her research in her dissertation, entitled “Kanien’kéha Through the Eyes of a First-Language Speaker.”


And along the way, she also became a peer mentor to some of those twenty-something-aged students who she was once intimidated to join.


She recently invited reporters to meet some of her young peers, who were gathering to discuss their research. She chatted with a young man in Mohawk, and gave advice to another student who was presenting to the group. McDonald jokingly refers to the group as fellow “super-nerds.”


Jessica Coon, the program director for the ad hoc graduate program in Indigenous language revitalization, was one of McDonald’s supervisors. Coon said McDonald’s contribution to the program is “hard to overstate.”


“As a thesis supervisor, I think we always get to learn something from our students, but this has never been more true than in the case of working with Mary because she just knows so much about the language,” she said in an interview.


She said the program was created in part to accommodate students whose interest in language revitalization spans different disciplines — such as linguistics and education, in McDonald’s case.


“We really want the program to be broad enough to accommodate students approaching language revitalization of their languages from a variety of different perspectives and to have the flexibility built in to do that across different disciplines,” she said.


She says another student graduated with McDonald at the Master’s level, and there are four more students who started this fall, including two more PhD candidates. McDonald “is the first, but she won’t be the last,” she said.


While McDonald now describes herself as “retired,” she is clearly keeping busy. She travels back to McGill every two weeks, where she serves as an elder in residence and meets with the research group.


She also still works with more advanced Mohawk language-learners, pushing them to expand the bounds of their abilities and express themselves with not only accuracy, but “pizzazz.”


She said she plans to keep building on her thesis, and writing down the concepts she has spent a lifetime studying.


“I’ll do this till the day I pass because it’s a lot of fun,” she said.


Story by Morgan Lowrie

author: Clara Saliba
title: Está na hora de falar da pobreza de tempo
content:
Chegamos em novembro. As lojas e praças já estão decoradas para o Natal. No ar, a sensação de que o tempo passa rápido demais, de que nos atropela… Em meio às reflexões de quase fim de ano, reparei que o tempo, desta vez, esteve mais em pauta do que nunca. Afinal, reduzimos a jornada de trabalho e acabamos com a escala 6×1. 


Ainda este ano, em 16 de dezembro, os trabalhadores e trabalhadoras sob o regime CLT terão direito a duas folgas semanais. Também na mesma data, 60 dias após a aprovação da Emenda Constitucional 141, começará a valer o limite de jornada de 42h semanais, que cairá para 40h em dezembro de 2027. A única exceção à lei são os portadores de diploma de ensino superior que recebam mais de duas vezes e meia o teto do Regime Geral da Previdência Social (RGPS) – cerca de R$21 mil mensais. 


Uma conquista e tanto, que colocou no centro do debate público um número que não é monetário. Talvez pela primeira vez na história, falou-se tanto sobre um valor que não vem sempre acompanhado de um cifrão: o tempo das pessoas. 


Sim, tempo é, em certa medida, dinheiro. Sobretudo para a classe trabalhadora, as horas de vida que se gasta trabalhando têm uma relação importante com a possibilidade de pagar as contas ao fim do mês. 


Frequentemente, terceirizamos algumas tarefas porque é mais fácil pagar por elas do que dispor das horas para fazê-las. 


Quem nunca escolheu comer um salgado pronto, no caminho para o trabalho, apenas para poder dormir mais meia hora, e não se preocupar em preparar o café da manhã? Ou contratou uma diarista, para dar conta da faxina que acumulava para o fim de semana? 


Mas essas duas variáveis não são a mesma coisa: ainda que ter tempo nos economize dinheiro – permitindo que nós mesmas realizemos uma série de tarefas em vez de pagar por elas – e que ter dinheiro nos economize tempo – permitindo que contratemos – nem todo o dinheiro do mundo substitui a necessidade de tempo para comer, dormir, ter higiene e socializar, por exemplo. E nem todo o tempo, se não virar dinheiro, nos torna autossuficientes materialmente.


Esse é o raciocínio por trás de uma medida econômica pouco conhecida, e que tem sido explorada pela economia feminista: a pobreza de tempo.  


A economista estadunidense Clair Vickery escreveu sobre isso nos anos 1977. Ela definiu como pobres de tempo as famílias que não teriam uma combinação mínima de tempo para realizar as tarefas de cuidado pessoal e doméstico e dinheiro para comprar bens essenciais. Nessa linha, quem tem menos dinheiro precisa compensar com tempo, e quem tem menos tempo, com dinheiro. Quem não consegue nenhuma combinação suficiente de dinheiro e tempo com o salário que recebe é pobre, mesmo que ganhe mais do que o mínimo da linha de pobreza monetária. 


Nessa pesquisa, ela identificou as mães e pais “solo” como a população mais vulnerável à pobreza de tempo, ainda que essa situação seja mais comum entre as mulheres. Muitas vezes, elas estão sobrecarregadas pelo cuidado dos filhos, acumulando a jornada de trabalho fora com a responsabilidade total por outra(s) pessoa(s). 


Aqui no Brasil, ainda é difícil mensurar a pobreza de tempo, porque nos falta uma variável indispensável dessa equação: saber quantas horas as pessoas gastam por dia em cada atividade, o que é conhecido como pesquisa de “Uso do Tempo”. O que sabemos são quantas horas as pessoas passam trabalhando fora de casa por semana. Sabemos também, em alguma medida, quanto tempo elas gastam em cuidados e afazeres domésticos: 21 horas para as mulheres e 11 para os homens, de acordo com o IBGE, em 2022, ainda que haja fortes indícios de que essa pesquisa erre para baixo. As médias dos outros países da América Latina para mulheres, por exemplo, ficam sempre acima das 30h (para saber mais, vale ler a

Nota de Política Econômica 64 do Made-USP

). 


Mas, mesmo que seja difícil de medir,

a pobreza de tempo certamente é experienciada por muitos brasileiros e brasileiras. 


Longas horas no transporte público e jornadas elevadas de trabalho dentro e fora de casa se traduzem em uma qualidade de vida que despenca. 


Soma-se a isso todos os problemas de elevação do custo de vida percebidos desde a pandemia, e o resultado é que nem a renda nem o tempo tem sido suficientes para muitas pessoas, especialmente para as mulheres.


O tamanho da mobilização pela redução da jornada de trabalho foi uma prova disso.

 A aprovação da PEC com unanimidade na Câmara e no Senado não deixou dúvidas:

no debate público …

author: anred
title: Triple lesbicidio de Barracas: llega el veredicto y movilizan a Tribunales para exigir que se reconozca el crimen de odio
content:
Foto: Ariel Gutraich / Archivo Agencia Presentes.


A más de dos años del ataque incendiario en una habitación de una pensión de Barracas, este miércoles 18 de noviembre se conocerá el veredicto del juicio por el triple lesbicidio de Barracas. La Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más convoca a concentrarse desde las 9 frente al Palacio de Tribunales para exigir que la sentencia contra Justo Fernando Barrientos reconozca el ataque como un crimen de odio por orientación sexual e identidad de género.

La fiscalía y las querellas solicitaron prisión perpetua, mientras que la defensa pidió la absolución del acusado y, subsidiariamente, que se descarten los agravantes. El proceso busca establecer la responsabilidad penal por el ataque que terminó con la vida de Andrea Amarante, Pamela Cobbas y Roxana Figueroa y dejó gravemente herida a Sofía Castro Riglos.

 Por ANRed.


Este miércoles 18 de noviembre se conocerá el veredicto del juicio por el triple lesbicidio de Barracas.

La Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más convoca a concentrarse desde las 9 frente al Palacio de Tribunales para exigir que la sentencia contra Justo Fernando Barrientos reconozca el ataque como un crimen de odio por orientación sexual e identidad de género

. La fiscalía y las querellas solicitaron prisión perpetua, mientras que la defensa pidió la absolución del acusado.


La audiencia ante el Tribunal Oral en lo Criminal y Correccional N° 5 comenzará a las 9:30 con las respuestas de las acusaciones a los planteos de la defensa y las últimas palabras del imputado. La lectura del veredicto está prevista para las 11.

La convocatoria invita a organizaciones, activistas y a toda la comunidad a acompañar la jornada y reclamar justicia por Andrea Amarante, Pamela Cobbas y Roxana Figueroa, además de justicia y reparación para Sofía Castro Riglos, única sobreviviente del ataque

.


Imagen: archivo Perycia.


El hecho ocurrió durante la madrugada del 6 de mayo de 2024, en una habitación de una pensión ubicada en la calle Olavarría al 1600, en el barrio porteño de Barracas. Allí vivían las cuatro mujeres lesbianas, que compartían un espacio habitacional en un contexto de precariedad económica y habitacional. Según la acusación, Barrientos, vecino del lugar que había protagonizado episodios previos de hostigamiento y amenazas, arrojó un artefacto incendiario contra la habitación. Como consecuencia del ataque, Andrea, Pamela y Roxana murieron, mientras que Sofía sobrevivió con graves secuelas.


Durante el juicio oral, que comenzó el 18 de mayo de este año, las querellas y la fiscalía sostuvieron que el ataque estuvo motivado por el odio hacia la orientación sexual de las víctimas. Los testimonios de vecinas y allegadas reconstruyeron las situaciones de hostigamiento que atravesaban las mujeres, mientras que las pericias de bomberos y especialistas apuntaron a que el incendio fue intencional.

Las acusaciones solicitaron prisión perpetua y reclamaron que se contemplen los agravantes de odio por orientación sexual y de género, junto con los restantes agravantes penales

.


Imagen: archivo Enfant Terrible.


Una de las particularidades del proceso fue la participación de

una querella colectiva impulsada por la Federación Argentina LGBT (FALGBT+)

, que representa a la comunidad en el juicio. Su intervención constituye un antecedente inédito en un debate judicial de estas características y fue posible luego de que la Cámara de Casación habilitara su incorporación, tras anteriores rechazos durante la etapa de instrucción.


Por su parte, la defensa de Barrientos, encabezada por

Ricardo Antonio Richiello

, pidió la absolución por el beneficio de la duda y cuestionó las pruebas testimoniales y periciales presentadas durante el debate. De manera subsidiaria, solicitó que se descarte la aplicación de los agravantes de odio y violencia de género y que, en caso de una condena, se considere una figura penal menos grave. También cuestionó la constitucionalidad de la prisión perpetua y las medidas de reparación económica reclamadas para Sofía.


Imagen: Agencia Presentes.


Desde la Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más remarcaron que el reclamo excede la determinación de la responsabilidad penal del acusado: «Exigimos que la causa se nombre como lesbicidio y que la sentencia contemple el agravante de odio por orientación sexual e identidad de género, además de la violencia de género».

author: CMI Argentina
title: Recuerdos del futuro del fentanilo
content:
El fentanilo surgió de las farmacias y sanatorios de Estados Unidos como una oferta auspiciada por ese estado y construyó el mercado consumidor millonario en personas y multimillonario en dólares. Las muertes por fentanilo son consecuencia de un negocio paraestatal y multinacional.


Donald Trump inventa carteles en Venezuela para quedarse con el petróleo y lo seguirá haciendo en México, Brasil, Argentina y Colombia para explotar de manera irracional los bienes comunes de los pueblos del sur.


En su reinvención de la historia apela a los principios de la guerra fría, las doctrinas de seguridad nacional y continental.


Hacer de los ejércitos de los pueblos por debajo del Río Bravo los guardianes pretorianos de la concentración y extranjerización de riquezas con la excusa del combate al narcotráfico.


Lo lleva adelante con la complicidad de los presidentes electos por el voto popular aunque cada vez es más notorio que el capitalismo desprecia esas formas republicanas.


En esa revisión del relato norteamericano, Trump falsifica los hechos que dieron origen a uno de los principales problemas sanitarios del pueblo de los Estados Unidos que es el mercado negro del fentanilo.


El actual presidente acusa a los carteles mexicanos de los hijos del Chapo Guzmán de ser los causantes de la epidemia cuyos efectos pueden verse en distintos sitios de Youtube, personas degradadas a ser zombis que deambulan sin sentido en las principales calles del imperio.


La realidad histórica es que el fentanilo emergió de las farmacias y sanatorios de Estados Unidos como una oferta auspiciada por el estado norteamericano y construyó el mercado consumidor millonario en personas y multimillonario en dólares.


Las muertes por fentanilo son consecuencia del negocio del fentanilo, paraestatal y multinacional, como lo es el narcotráfico, la venta de armas, los medicamentos, la trata de personas y ciertas vertientes del increíble comercio del petróleo y derivados.


Cuando aparecieron las muertes por fentanilo contaminado en Argentina, las diferentes dimensiones de la justicia apuntaron a lotes que se perdieron de su trazabilidad.


Lo cierto es que mientras avanza el tiempo van apareciendo noticias que confirman la repetición de aquellas etapas del negocio tal cual surgió y se consolidó en Estados Unidos.


Desde los laboratorios, sanatorios, hospitales y farmacias a las calles, al surgimiento y posterior consolidación de un mercado negro de fentanilo que será la base del consumo de miles de personas.


El 23 de octubre de 2026, fueron allanados tres sanatorios de Rosario por la venta ilegal de fentanilo y morfina.


“La investigación sobre la venta y uso ilegal de fentanilo y morfina en Wheelwright se actualizó después de cuatro meses. La Justicia federal ordenó una serie de allanamientos en tres sanatorios de Rosario para profundizar la pesquisa que comenzó con una denuncia de fraude en Pami.


La Policía Federal Argentina (PFA) inspeccionó distintos centros de salud privados de la ciudad y también de Acebal. Esta última es una de las dos localidades donde se enfocó la causa penal por el suministro ilícito de los fármacos por parte de un médico y un enfermero. En total, el Ministerio Público Fiscal (MPF) solicitó ocho allanamientos en busca de evidencia. De esta manera se secuestraron medicamentos sin recetas como diazepam, ondansetrón y dexametasona. Además, los encargados del procedimiento identificaron a siete nuevos sospechosos vinculados con la causa que tomó estado público a principios de junio en el departamento General López. La División Unidad Operativa de Investigaciones Especiales (DUOIE) de la PFA fue a las oficinas de los sanatorios Norte, Laprida y Delta. También revisaron inmuebles particulares de Rosario y una farmacia de Acebal, entre otros domicilios”, informaron los medios de comunicación regionales.


Esta información va repitiéndose no solamente en la provincia de Santa Fe sino también en otros lugares de la Argentina.


El fentanilo no es consecuencia de una “tragedia”, si no de la planificación de un negocio a escala internacional y cuya matriz está en los Estados Unidos.


Fuente: Diario “La Capital”, Rosario, viernes 23 de octubre de 2026; “Geografía narco 10”, del autor de esta nota.
