author: Rebecca John
title: Big Oil, Climate Change, and a ‘Smoking Gun’
content:
Arnold Obguia did not leave the island. According to the forecast, it was no big deal, just another tropical storm. But a few hours later, the winds escalated rapidly, bringing waves so large they almost pulled him out to sea. Clinging to a piece of broken sea wall, Arnold survived to find his house completely destroyed. Others were not so lucky.


This story is published in partnership with

Rolling Stone.


Typhoon Rai, known locally as Typhoon Odette, battered the Philippines in December 2021. With winds of up to 167 miles per hour, extreme rainfall, violent storm surges, extensive flooding, and landslides across the central Philippine archipelago, Odette ripped rooftops from houses and devastated crops, engulfing people and property in torrents of fast-flowing floodwater. A Category 5 cyclone, Odette displaced nearly

3.2 million people

, killing 400, injuring over 1,000, and causing nearly a billion US dollars in damages.


Now, Arnold and other victims of the typhoon are demanding their day in court, filing a civil

lawsuit

 against

oil and gas giant Shell

. Their allegations: Shell helped to make the typhoon more destructive through the company’s contribution to historic greenhouse gas emissions and its funding of climate denial — despite knowing since at least 1965 that the burning of fossil fuels was the primary cause of man-made climate change.


“The forecast had initially said it was going to be a weak storm,” says Arnold from the house he rebuilt with storm debris on the tiny island of Bilangbilangan in the heart of the Philippines’ Cebu Strait. Forty-four years old, Arnold is a fisherman, born and raised on the island, who earns his living catching trevally and bigeye scad, silvery-blue-green fish that swim in large schools around the region’s coral reefs.


“But suddenly the winds were different, they were very strong,” he recalls. “When I looked outside the window it was frightening because the waves were very high.” While his wife and two young daughters had taken refuge on the mainland, Arnold and his 14-year-old son had stayed behind to guard his boat and fishing equipment — the source of the family’s livelihood. “The waves were swelling and I could see the storm surge coming,” he remembers. Calculating that he might have time to better secure his boat, he ran outside only to get caught by the 20-foot waves that nearly swept him away. Terrified, Arnold held tight to the broken sea wall until, bruised and wounded by the debris whirling in the water, he was able to rejoin his son. “Thinking about my family and how much I wanted to see them again gave me the strength to hold on,” he says. Arnold and his son rode out the rest of the storm sheltering in the house of a neighbor. Hours later, when it was over, Arnold discovered his boat was broken but his family was safe. Like everyone else on Bilangbilangan, they had lost almost all their possessions. “Everyone went back to zero,” he explains.


Arnold joined the lawsuit in early 2024 when a coalition of NGOs working with communities ravaged by the typhoon organized a

civil claim

 on behalf of the survivors. In 2025, British law firm Hausfeld agreed to take up the case in the UK — where Shell is headquartered —submitting full details of the claim against the oil company in July of this year.


Typhoon Rai — known as Odette in the Philippines — had sustained winds of 121 miles (195 kilometers) and gusts of up to 167 miles (270 kilometers) per hour when it made landfall in the archipelago on December 16, 2021. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE , GIBS/Worldview , and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership. Public Domain.


Representing more than 100 of the typhoon’s victims, Hausfeld describes the suit as a “landmark case” that could have “major repercussions for the

fossil fuel industry,

” potentially paving the way for other hard-hit communities around the world to sue oil Big Oil on its home turf. The firm argues its clients suffered severe losses including serious property damage, personal injury, bereavement, psychological trauma, and loss of earnings. An announcement of the date for the first hearing to be held at London’s High Court is expected sometime early next year, says Greg Lascelles, the Hausfeld partner leading the legal team.


Shell has dismissed

the lawsuit

 as “baseless,” asserting the company had no “unique knowledge about climate change” in an

official …

author: winter oak
title: Chinese communism and the usual suspects
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article

here


The seizure of power by the communists in 1949 led to a brutal and murderous assault on Chinese life that was even worse than that experienced by Russians under the Bolsheviks.


In January 1958 Mao Zedong, the chairman of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), launched the regime’s second five-year plan, known as the Great Leap Forward.


Says


Wikipedia

: “The purpose of the plan was to use heavy industry to expedite the production of raw materials such as steel as a supplement to economic growth, similar to the Soviet model and the defining factor behind Mao’s Chinese Marxist policies.


“Mao spent ten months touring the country in 1958 to gain support for the Great Leap Forward and inspect the progress that had already been made. What this entailed was the humiliation, public castigation and torture of all who questioned the leap”. [1]


This rapid industrial “growth” and “development”, with people being sucked from the countryside into the cities, was a disaster – millions died from the resulting famine.


Author Frank Dikötter puts the death toll from 1958 to 1962 at more than 45 million Chinese – of these, around 7% were tortured and killed by the government, 2% committed suicide and 5% died in Mao’s labour camps built to hold dissidents. [2]


He describes severe punishments for slight infractions, such as being buried alive for stealing a handful of grain or losing an ear and being branded for digging up a potato.


The so-called

Cultural Revolution

, which began in 1966, was an insanely cruel effort to impose “modernisation” and destroy all that was traditional.


Mao’s Red Guards sought to wipe out the “Four Olds” (old ideas, old culture, old customs, and old habits), often by desecrating historical artifacts and cultural and religious sites. Tens of millions of people were persecuted and sometimes massacred – up to 2 million died. [3]


I have previously explained how the

Bolshevik

,

Fascist

 and

Nazi

 regimes – which likewise combined rabid industrialism with authoritarian terror – were all controlled by the entity I call ZIM, the zio-imperialist mafia. [4] But who could have been behind the nightmarish communist tyranny that subsequently took hold of China?


Yitzhak Shichor of the University of Haifa and Hebrew University of Jerusalem sheds some light on the matter in a fascinating

paper

 published in the

International Journal of China Studies

 in 2020.


He writes: “Jews were deeply involved in Communist revolutions in Europe, and primarily in Russia, often in leading positions. This is understandable given their demographic location, extensive education and suffering over the years.


“However, how could we account for the fact that they also played a role in Communist revolutions in Asia, and especially in China? There were practically no Jewish communities to speak of and those few who lived there had been almost totally assimilated, and had no interest whatsoever in Chinese culture, history and politics.


“Still, Jews (who arrived out of China) not only took part in the revolution but had also helped igniting it and then stayed on or joined later”. [5]


Shichor (

pictured

) says of these Jewish participants: “Their main value to the revolution was mainly writing, translation, communication and publication. Although they were all deeply committed to the Chinese Communist revolution, some of them were jailed – for years – and occasionally more than once. Nonetheless, they continued to believe in, and even to justify, the Chinese Communist Party”. [6]


Shichor explains that the Marxist brand of socialism, which reached China via Japan, was initially

the least attractive

 to Chinese intellectuals.


“Considered too violent, the notions of ‘class struggle’ contradicted traditional Confucian values of harmonious and integrative society, and the thought that ‘workers’ represented the ‘universal’ and ‘revolutionary’ class, did not conform to pre-modern Chinese beliefs…


“Whatever socio-political opposition and ideological radicalism existed, they were articulated not by Marxist communism, but by anarchism. Mao Zedong, one of the founders and later leader of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), regarded himself as anarchist up to the early 1920s”. [7]


But Marxism-Leninism soon came to the fore, thanks to the influence of the Bolsheviks, and Schichor reveals that “many of the chief Soviet and Comintern missionaries in China were Jewish”. [8] …

author: Jake Bittle
title: Tribes push back as Congress moves to fast-track energy projects
content:
After years of negotiation, Congress is on the cusp of passing a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill that would make it far easier to build power plants and electric transmission lines in the United States. The bill was negotiated by a bipartisan group of senators including Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse, a noted climate hawk, and Republican Mike Lee, an opponent of environmental regulation. It has picked up support from

clean


energy


advocates

 because it would promote more transmission lines to carry renewable power to cities, speed up review for solar and wind projects, and stop presidents from cancelling offshore wind farms. It has also been endorsed by many

conservative

,

business

, and

fossil fuel

 groups, who say it would cut down on environmental red tape and speed up natural gas pipelines.


The bill has

divided the climate movement

, separating groups focused on

decarbonization

 from those focused on endangered species protection and environmental justice, but the most influential opposition has come from tribal nations. The bill would weaken a historic preservation law that tribes often use to protect cultural and religious sites from development, and numerous prominent Indigenous nations and organizations have said it harms tribal sovereignty.


While the bill cleared a procedural hurdle in the Senate last week, it remains unclear whether it will pass there or in the House. The negotiators who framed the bill say they believe they

have the votes

, but a number of Democrats in both chambers have opposed the bill. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next Speaker of the House, has

criticized

 what he called the bill’s “failure to adequately protect tribal sovereignty.” Nevada senator Catherine Cortez Masto, who voted to advance the bill, has said she won’t

ultimately vote to pass it

, saying she “cannot ignore the concerns” of tribes in her state.


“Projects affecting tribal governments before were already fast-tracked, but now this allows for a super fast track,” said John Bathke, a member of the Navajo Nation, a former historic preservation officer for the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Reservation, and now a professor of Indigenous studies at San Diego City College.


The 1966 National Historic Preservation Act, passed in the wake of nationwide urban renewal efforts that demolished many old buildings, requires the federal government to consider the effect of construction projects on historic and cultural properties. (Most intact objects or properties that are more than 50 years old and have some kind of historical, cultural, or religious significance qualify under the law.) When you’re building a solar farm or a transmission line, that is a big undertaking: The area of review can extend for as much as 5 miles away from the project itself, and major transmission lines can be hundreds of miles long. Even if a project is visible a few miles away when you’re standing in a historic area, that still counts as a potential effect.


While tribal nations have control over infrastructure projects on their reservations, many tribes have cultural, religious, and political claims over areas that are outside their reservation boundaries. The historic preservation law is one of the only tools they have to stop or alter construction projects that might desecrate sacred territories or religious sites. 


“Even though a lot of these projects aren’t on reservation land, it’s part of their traditional homeland, it’s part of their spiritual landscape,” said Bathke. “That land still belongs to them and they belong to that land.”


Tribal nations have used this law to limit energy projects that they say would harm their sacred territories. In perhaps the best-known example, the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Indian Reservation

sued the federal government

 in 2010 over its approval of a 6,000-acre solar farm on federal land in California, one of the first such projects in the United States. The tribe argued that the project would destroy religious sites and buried remains and that the government had rubber-stamped it after just a few meetings. A court sided with the tribe and the solar developer nixed the project, moving to build on private farmland instead. (Bathke was the tribe’s historic preservation officer — the tribal official who helps with historic reviews — during the solar dispute.)


Supporters of clean energy development have long sought to reform the law. They argue that historic preservation review …

author: Paul Gregoire
title: Karina Lester: ‘AUKUS is a radioactive waste nightmare’
content:
The AUKUS public inquiry released its final report on November 4. The five commissioners presented some stark realities about the “defence” pact between Australia, Britain and the United States, which is supposed to deliver eight Australian-owned nuclear-powered submarines (SSN).

A key issue the inquiry has brought to the fore is radioactive waste storage.

The AUKUS commissioners identified a massive cost — an estimated $180 billion — that taxpayers will have to foot, to store the radioactive waste.

This is on top of the $368 billion for the eight SSNs, which the inquiry said are not guaranteed to ever turn up.

The AUKUS report said that this additional, and never referred to, $180 billion outlay brings the total cost of AUKUS to around half a trillion dollars. It also advised that Australia has already gifted $3 billion to US and British submarine shipbuilding yards, with no guarantee of a refund if the deal collapses.

AUKUS Public Inquiry commissioner Karina Lester said that First Nations communities are concerned about the radioactive waste management plan, as there is no indication of where the waste site for highly-enriched uranium will be. It also remains highly volatile for hundreds of thousands of years.

Pillar I of AUKUS also establishes the Submarine Rotational Force – West, which involves US and British SSNs rotating out of HMAS Stirling, off the coast of Perth from 2027.

Even if the Australian-owned SSNs do not materialise, the Americans will have their own here at the ready.

The AUKUS commissioners recommended scrapping the AUKUS submarine deal entirely.

While Australia is expected to store its own waste, it turns out that the US and Britain have a decades-long issue of not being able to store their own waste.

Sydney Criminal Lawyers spoke to Karina Lester, one of the AUKUS Commissioners, who is a second-generation survivor of the British nuclear testing at Emu Field in South Australia.

The Yankunytjatjara Anangu woman said many First Nations communities are concerned about how and where the radioactive waste is going to be buried on Country, along with the fears over a base in Port Kembla.

The Surrendering Australia: The AUKUS Deception report clarifies many of the concerns about AUKUS. Fellow commissioner Peter Garrett told the National Press Club that the $368 billion works out to be $33 million a day for the next 30 years. He noted an additional estimated $180 billion will go towards managing radioactive waste disposal — a largely unaddressed aspect of the AUKUS deal. This is of particular significance to First Nations peoples.

What did the inquiry uncover regarding the storage of radioactive waste?

The AUKUS Public Inquiry found that it will be Australia’s responsibility to store the nuclear waste produced by these nuclear-powered submarines. The detail is yet to be defined or worked through.

Currently, Australia is going through a consultation process run by the Australian Radioactive Waste Management Framework. Last week, it was having consultations, which will provide feedback and clarity around waste management. But this was not about site selection.

From a First Nations perspective, if the AUKUS agreement says it is Australia’s responsibility to store this nuclear waste, we are concerned it will be stored somewhere in the outback, as we heard from former minister Kim Beazley. This, of course, will be First Nations traditional lands. So we are concerned about this.

At this stage, there is no site for the waste. But we’ve heard from defence minister Richard Marles that it will be somewhere on defence land, or future defence land. But there are no guidelines around where that future defence land will be.

At this stage, we know that we are responsible for the nuclear waste. This will be weapons’ grade nuclear waste, which will be concerning, as the waste will be high level and out on First Nations traditional lands.

So, there are unknowns coming out of the public inquiry and one of those is the site for nuclear waste.

When Marles refers to “future defence land”, does this mean that they could choose anywhere that is not currently defence land?

Yes. And there are no guidelines or criteria around how that selection process is going to be done, or where the future Defence land could be.

As Traditional Owners in South Australia, we have what is known as the Woomera Prohibited Area. That area is south of where my traditional lands are.

I’m up on the Anangu Pitjantjatjara …

author: Publicación Abierta
title: El genocidio indígena de la «Campaña del Desierto» llegó a los tribunales argentinos
content:
Boletín de pueblos originarios a 534 años de la invasión europea


El genocidio indígena de la «Campaña del Desierto» llegó a los tribunales argentinos


Mario Hernandez


 


El genocidio a los pueblos originarios de la Patagonia en el marco de la Campaña del Desierto (1878-1890) llegó a la Justicia argentina. El 16 de agosto, Ivana Noemí Huenelaf, mujer mapuche-tehuelche, presentó la denuncia ante los Tribunales Federales de Retiro (Ciudad de Buenos Aires). Lo hizo junto a su abogado Fernando Cabaleiro, de la ONG Naturaleza de Derechos. “Para que se inicie un Juicio por la Verdad a los fines que se investigue la comisión de hechos atroces que encuadran dentro de la figura de genocidio: torturas, fusilamientos, desapariciones forzadas y abandono de personas, apremios ilegales, traslados forzosos, disposición y reducción a servidumbre de personas y sustracción de menores”, dice el texto de la denuncia, que tiene 80 páginas.


Lxs demandantes pidieron que “en ese marco procesal se dicte una sentencia declarativa en referencia a todo ese proceso como un Genocidio y se dispongan las medidas y actos reparatorios que por derecho correspondan”.


 


El sorteo de rigor hizo recaer la denuncia en la Fiscalía 7 (González) y en el Juzgado en lo Criminal y Correccional Federal 3, (a cargo de Daniel Rafecas) de los tribunales federales de Retiro.


“Hay jueces  fiscales que nos pueden escuchar”


“Mari, mari”, saluda Huenelaf al salir de los Tribunales de Comodoro Py. “Siento el Newen (fuerza espiritual) porque es muy importante para mi pueblo. Se va tejiendo esto. Hay jueces y fiscales que nos pueden llegar a escuchar, es un gran paso que se gesta con la resistencia. No venimos con rabia sino con dolor para sanar esas heridas, con la sabiduría y el conocimiento de la Mapu (Madre Tierra), con gente que cree en nuestra causa”, dice con calma y sonriente esta mujer indígena. Y aclara: “No es sólo una etnia sino todos en comunidad, con Norita Cortiñas que va a ser testigo de concepto si nos aceptan como querella. Su genocidio fueron 30 mil víctimas, el nuestro fueron 20 mil, van a tener que acostumbrarse a ese número”, agrega Huenelaf.


Tiene 49 años, es madre de seis hijos y abuela de siete nietos. Nació en un paraje al pie de la Cordillera, José de San Martín. Es mapuche y tehuelche, y acompaña las recuperaciones de territorio. Vive en Mallín Ahogado, en un territorio en comunidad llamado Tierra y Dignidad. Trabaja en la feria regional donde vende pan casero y es profesora de judo –primer Dan– de niñeces en Lago Puelo.


En la soleada mañana del martes 16 de agosto, llevaba su vestimenta originaria y un brillante trarilonco (cintillo) de plata sobre el pelo negro azabache. Le trajo problemas. “Ni bien entré (a los tribunales) me demoraron. Hice tres pasos y una policía me agarró para no dejarme ingresar. Con mucha tranquilidad lo tomamos, tenemos medio naturalizado que nos paren y nos discriminen por portación de rostro. Hubo un cruce de palabras entre la policía y mi abogado pero finalmente pasamos a hacer lo que veníamos a hacer”, relata.


Desde la Campaña del desierto hasta Benetton


Ivana estuvo en enero de 2017 entre la decena de personas que acudió solidaria a la Lof en Resistencia de Cushamen cuando sus miembros fueron reprimidos por Gendarmería. Con ferocidad, como durante el operativo de agosto de aquel año, cuando desapareció el tatuador anarquista Santiago Maldonado.


Nunca imaginaron la pesadilla que vivieron después, al ser baleadas, perseguidas y detenidas. Ivana y el grupo fueron tiroteados por policías de Chubut y empleados de Benetton. Ella sacó fotos y logró avisar a una abogada, poco antes de ser golpeada y detenida en la comisaría de El Maitén. Mientras tanto, el fiscal Carlos Díaz Mayer negaba una y otra vez que estuvieran allí.  Se habrían quedado mucho tiempo más si no las sacaba el abogado Carlos “Chuzo” González Quintana que andaba por la zona de vacaciones.


“Me tocó vivir un proceso con una estrategia no muy diferente a la de 1879 que comenzó el genocidio que hoy estamos denunciando en Comodoro Py”, dice Huenelaf. El colmo fue que todas estas víctimas terminaron acusadas por el empresario italiano de robo de ganado y posesión de explosivos. Años más tarde quedaron absueltas: les habían plantado las pruebas. Así funcionan algunas cosas en la Patagonia.


“En razón de mi descendencia mapuche tehuelche”


“En razón de mi descendencia mapuche tehuelche, y siendo que los hechos cuya investigación …

author: dialogocomospovos
title: Somos Filhos do Tempo
content:
Durante a visita de Moira Millán ao Assentamento Terra Vista, em meio ao intercâmbio com lideranças Guarani, Kaiowá e Terena e à segunda etapa do Curso de Filosofia da Terra, a liderança mapuche aprofundou sua formação sobre a luta do povo Mapuche.


Em outro momento, Moira abordou a liderança como algo que não se reduz a figuras humanas: “O povo Mapuche não tem liderança humana. A liderança é a terra. A terra diz o que temos que fazer”, afirmou, explicando que esse dizer se manifesta por sonhos, sinais e pelo animar da vida. Para ela, os povos indígenas vivem mais de um plano de existência e enxergam além da terra tangível.


A organização social mapuche, disse, é horizontal e circular, e cada pessoa nasce com um propósito e um espírito preparado para cumpri-lo — como as mulheres e homens medicina. O cacique, nesse horizonte, não decide nem é o líder: aconselha e organiza com a gente. Moira também refletiu sobre a Ateja, espaço de identidade e memória que não se limita à produtividade.


Criticando a cultura dominante, que diz que somos filhos da história, ela propôs outra compreensão: “A história é um segmento, um retalho de narrativa que os humanos contam”. Ser filho do tempo, para os Mapuche, é algo muito mais longo e profundo — outro conceito de tempo-espaço.

author: Chantal Eco
title: Will the new FPIC guidelines fast-track the Pax Silica hub in ancestral lands?
content:
Indigenous Aytas from different villages in Capas, Tarlac, listen to an environmental advocate during a community gathering on August 16, 2026, to discuss the impacts of the proposed Pax Silica hub on their land. Photo by Chantal Eco / Bulatlat

“It was really built to cater to corporations. Any semblance that it protects IP rights and allows Indigenous peoples to say no is gone.”

Mandor Matias, 45, has lived all his life on his family’s land in Sitio Binyayan in Capas, Tarlac. He and his relatives plant rice and vegetables on about three hectares of land. But on July 15, employees from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) came to his house. They pointed to the planted land in front of it, handed him a paper to sign and offered P30 (USD 0.47) per square meter, or about P900,000 (US$ 14,100) for all three hectares.

“They gave me a paper and asked me to sign it. I said I didn’t need to sign it. If I signed it, it would be as if I had accepted payment,” Matias told Bulatlat in Filipino.

He was not told why they were being pushed to sell their land. He later learned through social media and then confirmed by their village head, that the Pax Silica hub, a U.S.-backed hub for artificial intelligence and semiconductor manufacturing, will be built on their land.

Matias is an indigenous Ayta. His home and farm now lie within the area of the proposed Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park, a 1,620-hectare hub in New Clark City that the BCDA is developing with the United States under the Pax Silica framework. Their fate may now be decided under new consent rules. In May, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) approved the contentious amendments to the guidelines on free, prior and informed consent (FPIC), and a copy was only released publicly in September. The 2026 guidelines shorten deadlines, approve permits automatically when officials fail to act on time, and let some government projects pass with a document review instead of a full community vote. Indigenous groups warn the rules could clear the way for Pax Silica and other “development projects” on ancestral lands.

The FPIC process could take months to years, especially when a project could greatly affect the ancestral land and the community is divided. The new FPIC guidelines run on tight deadlines: seven working days for the NCIP’s field investigation, 10 days for community assemblies on large projects and up to 60 days for the community to decide. If NCIP officials fail to act on time on a completed consent report, the certificate is issued automatically.

Government-funded projects need only a document review if they are “non-commercial.” Those with private partners or long-term impacts go to Category A or B, as the regional director decides. Projects that displace residents fall under Category A, the strictest track. But a project can get its certificate even before it is clear which households will be affected. Protections for those families can be settled later. Meanwhile, even after a community says no, the applicant keeps the right to refile.

Funa-ay Claver, an Indigenous youth leader and spokesperson of Katribu, said the BCDA may avoid FPIC altogether by insisting that no Indigenous people live on the site.

“It was really built to cater to corporations. Any semblance that it protects IP rights and allows Indigenous peoples to say no is gone,” Claver explained in Filipino.

She said the categories depend on a project’s scale, not on how many people it affects, and that manufacturing hubs are not mentioned anywhere. She added that the NCIP never released a draft for public comment.

Katribu said it is wary of even calling on the BCDA to “uphold FPIC.” Under the new rules, Claver said, consent risks becoming a checklist that only clears the way for the project.

At a media forum of the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP) in September, BCDA President Joshua Bingcang claimed that they have always consulted communities whenever there’s a project or development within New Clark City. While showing pictures of what he described as consultations, he did not specifically say that they have already consulted, much less secured the consent of the Aytas living in the area where the Pax Silica hub will be built.

He called the hub site “already BCDA property” and promised, “We will not just kick them out… there will be consultations.”

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: ‘It’s all about taking care of people’: How a smǝlqmíx farmer is building food sovereignty at ntámłqən
content:
Dixon Terbasket, the founder of ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands, walks through the farm’s greenhouse on Sept. 15, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


The potato plants are so tall that their stems reach Dixon Terbasket’s eyes.


He remembers walking through his family’s garden when he was three or four years old, more than 60 years ago, in a community where his mom, all his aunties and uncles, grew food in gardens and orchards — and stored them in root cellars, too.


Now, Dixon finds himself leading his own food sovereignty initiative that he hopes will equip the next generation of smǝlqmíx (Similkameen) people with the knowledge and skills to farm on their own.


“I want to give them at least a running chance, man,” Dixon told IndigiNews.


The ntámłqən garden is in unceded smǝlqmíx territory in the lower Similkameen Valley, in the southern Interior of “B.C.” It shares its nsyilxcən name with the adjacent community elementary school, meaning “gathering place.” Dixon said his people have gathered here since time immemorial.


The ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens


At ntámłqən, a 7.5-acre community garden and food hub on Lower Similkameen Indian Band (LSIB) land near “Cawston,” he works with a small but dedicated crew of staff and volunteers to teach people life skills — from growing their own food; to sharing it with the community; and how to preserve what they grow.


At the peak of the harvest season, the garden hosted a free barbeque for the community on Sept. 28, in collaboration with the Indigenous Food Sovereignty Association. 


Rumy Muenala helps prepare food for a community BBQ at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Staff at ntámłqən Community Garden prepare salads during a community BBQ event at the farm in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Dozens of people — Indigenous and non-Indigenous — came together around meals made with ingredients provided by the garden and its partners. Between all the mingling and laughs, they feasted on stuffed-peppers, colourful salads, watermelon, goat meat, apple pie and more.


“It’s all about taking care of people,” Dixon said, echoing the farm’s slogan of “For The People.”


Hannah Field, who co-manages the ntámłqən Community Garden as its coordinator, stands in a prayer circle before a community BBQ event at the farm in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Community members fill their plates with food during a community BBQ event hosted at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


The garden is working towards giving the community the ability to make decisions about their food — and having the knowledge, land and facilities to provide for one another. A processing facility expected to be completed by March 2027 will add space to prepare and store harvests, with opportunities for community food businesses. 


Dixon’s niece, Coven Terbasket, joined the crew in 2024, a couple of weeks after moving back to her ancestral homelands. She was 29 and looking for work when she ran into Dixon at an insurance office in small-town Keremeos. 


For most of her life, Coven had lived south of the colonial border in “Spokane, Washington.” During childhood summers, her mom would send her up to “roam around” LSIB lands with family, usually in their ancestral community of nkʷrulauxʷ (Blind Creek, Place of Yellow Dirt). 


Like her uncle, she remembers family gardens all around Blind Creek, and the work that kept households fed beyond the growing season.


“Everyone had made the time to grow their own food, can their own food, to preserve,” she said.


Coven Terbasket, the administrative assistant at the ntámłqən Community Garden, is pictured at the farm in smǝlqmíx homelands on Oct. 5, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Coven hadn’t seen Dixon since she was a child. As they reconnected in the insurance office two years ago, he learned she needed work and offered her a job at the community garden he had been building with a small crew of workers and volunteers for more than a year.


“He told me to show up at the garden the next day at 10 a.m., so I did,” she said.


Coven describes the encounter as fate, saying her uncle “found me” shortly after her return, during a difficult period in her life. 


“It’s freaky how crazy it worked out … me looking for a job; me …

author: Nina Garcia Steel
title: Crossing Dimensions of Pain Without Losing My Soul
content:
A

s I sit here in my—as I like to call it—Oasis in the Desert, looking out my window at the morning clouds gloriously dancing to the tune the songbirds sing every morning is simply a treasure. I can smile at the sun and sway with the wind as it tickles my senses. I enjoy this morning view as I sip a cup of sweet herbal tea and take in the rays of light.


There was a time when such treasures were absent in my mind. I was living with undeniable pain that I could not explain, except in my poetry.


Photo by Nina Garcia Steel


It’s my heart that aches the most.


The feeling of nerves tearing and bones slowly breaking.


Flares of fire running through my veins.


The words that everyone took as metaphorical were literal words of agony from trauma that started decades earlier. It would take over half a century to discover the root cause of the autoimmune conditions that developed, the near dementia scares. At one point, I was having severe neurological attacks where I lost control of my limbs entirely, making them feel as though they were being tossed around like a rag doll. I picked three alcoholic husbands and stayed in abusive relationships. Little did I know that all of this was coming from the same place:

unprocessed trauma

.


It took me by surprise too. I had been making decisions about who I chose to be my mate based on what I thought was normal from what I experienced as a child. I had suffered sexual abuse more than once, starting when I was only 7 at the hands of a friend’s oldest brother, then an uncle who was visiting, with the worst culprit being my own father. What does a horrific experience like that do to the mind of an innocent child? Nobody was ever prosecuted, my therapy was abruptly stopped, and nothing was done. Left without justice or support, I was left to navigate the aftermath entirely on my own. This meant those early patterns quietly and unknowingly dictated my choices for years.


Decades later, the trauma manifested itself as depression. The connection wasn’t obvious because nobody asked the core question: What happened in your childhood?


So many individuals struggle with trauma that they cannot even name, for we are told, even by medical professionals, that we must focus on our future and that going backward is not in their school of thought. However, trauma is the poisonous seed that grows weeds of unnecessary pain that need to be destroyed at the root.


I walked with pride for so many years, challenging the status quo despite what had happened. I buried it without realizing that everything always comes back if not properly addressed. The pain of betrayal is doubly sharp when there’s unprocessed trauma in the background. It is unfortunate that the questions that could have shaped my treatment were not asked.


I always did things differently, even as early as 6 years old when I was selected to teach a kindergartener English, showing a precocious initiative and drive to bridge gaps long before I understood what systemic obstacles even were. I remember thinking that it was important for my student, Alicia, to learn hopscotch as that would make it easier for her to integrate with the other children. I was an ESL assistant from third to sixth grade. Selling shiny rocks door-to-door for ice-cream money at age 6, writing formal letters in Spanish to my grandfather at age 8. At just 14 years old, I served as the inventory buyer for our family shoe store. I was entrusted to travel on buying trips with an adult and curate the shoes for our inventory.


Learning the mechanics of commerce, spatial merchandising and inventory selection at such a young age taught me how to analyze systems, spot value, and exercise practical strategy long before I ever had to apply those skills to my own survival. At 15, that same drive led me to approach my high school principal with a proposal to redesign the school uniform. I saw how the existing uniforms lacked functionality and aesthetic timelessness, so I designed an updated, structurally timeless uniform that my school adopted. I was already practicing the art of seeing what needed change, organizing a solution, and taking decisive action.


I dared not dwell on the horror of the abuse I had experienced, not realizing that my body would keep score. At that stage, blocking the pain was pure survival. I hadn’t yet allowed my mind to acknowledge the true scope of what had happened — confronting it all at once would have destroyed me, so I compartmentalized …

author: Freedom Editor
title: Bullshit Burnham’s war on the disabled
content:
Andy Burnham promised an end to forty years of neoliberalism. Instead, he’s embraced the persecution of its favourite scapegoats

The news that the Milburn Review is to recommend the end of Personal Independence Payment (PIP), and the health element of Universal Credit for most young people under the age of 25, is not a surprise to those of us in the disability rights community, but it is horrific all the same.

According to Labour, it’s for their own good; no-one, intones Andy solemnly, wants to be trapped in a cycle of dependency, do they? Of course, this is all bullshit. Intentions matter, and neither the Milburn Review into the number of young people not in education, employment or training (NEET) or the Timms Review into PIP itself, were commissioned for the benefit of the young or the disabled, but for the benefit of the government’s bank balance.

Put simply—and no-one is questioning this—the number of claimants has increased significantly since the pandemic. One million young people are not in work or education. And the government doesn’t want to spend money on the problem.

But the clue is in the chronology. Though COVID has been memory-holed by many, not least government, which has worked assiduously to prevent Long COVID being recognised as a disability, the UK as elsewhere went through a once-in-a-century pandemic a handful of years ago. Apart from the death toll, which the COVID Inquiry acknowledges was worsened by government policy, many were left disabled and chronically ill.

That’s not the whole story, but it’s a big part of it, and as with COVID more generally it’s one government simply pretends doesn’t exist. The Burnham/Milburn rhetoric on disability is one of sympathy, that this is a ‘moral’ choice by government, that these ‘changes’ are an opportunity for a generational reset for young people who have, by Burnham’s own admission, been failed by politicians.

On that last we can agree, but Burnham’s no break with that catalogue of failure. Like his predecessors Starmer and Reeves, Burnham’s characterised PIP as an out-of-work benefit, when it is isn’t – it’s paid to ensure folks can be independent (the clue is in the name) and meet the additional costs which are incurred by being disabled in an ableist society. This is a wilful play into right-wing ‘scrounger’ rhetoric.

Burnham’s not wrong to mention that austerity had an enormous impact on the young in the coalition years, but lest we forget this is a man who lost a previous chance at the Labour leadership primarily because he refused to vote against coalition welfare cuts in 2015, a decision which fuelled a grassroots revolt in the Labour Party and the ultimate election of Jeremy Corbyn.

Indeed, what’s proposed here is a massive real-terms saving to government dressed up as empowerment for its victims—which is the classic Labour play. But anyone with any critical faculty can read Burnham’s words and know they are bullshit.

His constant references to parity of esteem in the education sector could have been written by any government, Labour or Tory, for the last sixty years. As with everything with him, it is surface-level, hoping to play on common-sensical shibboleths that will encourage folks to look past (or not at all at) the actual policy.

The same weekend his op-ed was published, a TikTok found its way online from the Labour account with Andy saying “we used to have a laugh…talk about pub snacks” before the Union Jack came prominently into play. The more things change, the more they stay the same, as the Burnham revolution boils down to idiotic chat about pork scratchings and pints whilst the young have what precious little support they get taken from them.

Labour’s messaging this week is to say that what they propose is more humane than what the Tories want to do, that they are offering a jobs guarantee and hope. But like all Burnham’s promises it’s a mirage. Milburn has proposed a reduction in employer national insurance for young people, but not yet; young people will still be paid less for the same work too.

Young people still won’t be able to access the mental health care they need. They will supposedly be able to apply to ‘local funds’ for support, funds which don’t exist and if they ever did based on prior experience would be unlikely to be responsive. But this rhetoric is just to salve the consciences of those not directly affected.

title: AKP ilçe başkanıyla görüşmeyen ilçe sağlık müdürüne "istifa" baskısı iddiası
content:
Rize – Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü görevinden alınan İ.Ö'nün, AKP Pazar İlçe Başkanı Furkan Namlı’nın ziyaret talebini kabul etmediği gerekçesiyle geçen günlerde istifaya zorlandığı iddia edildi. Yeni Parti Rize İl Başkanı Saltuk Deniz, İ.Ö'nün görevine iadesini isteyerek, AKP yetkililerine “Kurum amirleri sizin hizmetkârınız değildir” dedi.

Edinilen bilgilere göre, 4 Ağustos 2026 tarihinde AKP Pazar İlçe Başkanı olan Furkan Namlı ve beraberindeki yönetim kurulu üyeleri, kurum ziyaretleri kapsamında Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü’nden telefonla randevu talep etti. İlçe Sağlık Müdürü Dr. İ.Ö’nün ilk talebin ardından müsait olmadığını belirttiği, ikinci telefon görüşmesinde ise 657 sayılı Devlet Memurları Kanunu’na tabi bir kamu görevlisi olduğunu ifade ederek siyasi parti ilçe başkanlarıyla makamında görüşmeyeceğini bildirdiği ileri sürüldü.

Rize'deki AKP yetkililerince bunun İl Sağlık Müdürü Prof. Dr. Gökhan Demiral’a ileterek Dr. İ.Ö’nün görevden alınmasını ya da istifa etmesinin istendiği, bunun ardından Dr. İ.Ö’ye istifa etmesi yönünde telkinde bulunulduğu ancak ilçe sağlık müdürünün bunu kabul etmediği savunuldu.

Dr. İ.Ö. bir süre sonra ise İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü'nden alındı.

Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü çalışanları da Dr. İ.Ö’ye istifa etmesi yönünde baskı yapıldığını ifade etti.

Yeni Parti Rize İl Başkanı Saltuk Deniz, Dr. İ.Ö’nün Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü'nden alınmasına tepki gösterdi. Kamu kurumlarında görev yapan yöneticilerin siyasi parti temsilcilerinin hizmetinde olmadığını vurgulayan Deniz, şu açıklamayı yaptı:

“Devlet kurumlarında çalışan görevlilerimiz siyasi parti temsilcilerinin hizmetkârı değillerdir. Kurum amirleri, hiçbir siyasi parti temsilcisi ile görevleri dışında görüşmek zorunda değildir. Daha önce de benzeri olaylar ilimizde yaşanmıştı. Rize İl Milli Eğitim Müdürü Halil İbrahim Akmeşe de İl Milli Eğitim Müdürlüğü görevine atanır atanmaz, daha koltuğuna oturmadan soluğu AKP İl Başkanlığı’nda aldı. Bunlar doğru şeyler değildir. Kurum amirleri sizlerin hizmetkârı değildir. Rahat bırakın çalışanları. Kurumlarda iş barışını bozmanın, amirleri ve memurları siyasal gücünüzü kullanarak görevlerinden almak ya da uzaklaştırmakla diğer kurum çalışanlarına gözdağı vermenin siyasi ahlakla da bağdaşmadığını düşünüyoruz. AKP sözcülerini ve İl Sağlık Müdürlüğü’nü bu konuyla ilgili açıklama yapmalarını, görevinden alınan doktorumuzun yeniden görevine iade edilmesini kamuoyu adına talep ediyoruz.”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Petala Ironcloud
title: Native Youth Programs Are Building a Different Model of Mental Health Care
content:
These models are employing youth and grounding well-being in culture, relationships, and community.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Growing up in Eureka, a small city in Northern California, provided Roger “Chapreges” Jones an anchor in his Yurok culture. He took public K-12 Yurok language classes and Indian Ed covered school supplies. But when his parents divorced and he moved to Redding at 13, those resources vanished — and so did his appetite.

Chapreges got his first job at a Native American mental health clinic while grappling with an eating disorder hidden in plain sight. His new role at Two Feathers Native American Family Services became a kind of Trojan horse: He walked through the door looking for employment and found therapy waiting inside.

Founded in 1998 by a tribal consortium to strengthen Native family units in Humboldt County, Two Feathers has grown significantly since 2018, when its current executive director, Virgil Moorehead, joined. It went from having four staff members to having 32, including mental health clinicians, substance abuse counselors, and cultural coordinators.

Two Feathers serves a disproportionately large Native population across Northern California, where many Tribes and their citizens are either unrecognized federally or have been disenrolled. Critically, it serves Native families regardless of enrollment status — a stance that resists the disenrollment politics that plague underfunded tribes across Indian Country.

Chapreges is one of dozens of Native youth accessing Two Feathers services in a region where waitlists are long and federal funding cuts have gutted alternatives. A 2022 study from the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health echoes mounting research on the importance of cultural connection to Native youth’s mental health.

Chapreges’s experience speaks to that truth. He had struggled to acclimate to Redding without other Native youth or regular cultural resources beyond the annual Stillwater Powwow. In his sophomore year, he and his father, overwhelmed by the isolation, returned to Eureka, where Chapreges completed high school.

The following year, he became a youth ambassador at Two Feathers, promoting their culturally tailored programming: stick games, flower dance, trips to the local powwow, and the Young Bucks and Spotted Does programs for youth ages 8 to 12.

Moorehead is also a licensed clinical psychologist and has helmed a new era for the organization, implementing circular Native philosophy by creating a continuum of school- and family-oriented treatment services for Native youth and their families. Two Feathers’ approach reflects a broader Indigenous understanding of mental health that recognizes the effects of historical trauma while at the same time accounting for the distinct experiences of different Native communities.

One such program, the Acorn Youth Wellness Program, works with youth individually to bolster their cultural identity. “But I think giving them hope, you know, sense of belonging,” said Moorehead, “Those are all things that are measured.”

Moorehead said the program tracks attendance, cultural identity, and hope for the future. “I always say that if you don’t have kids that come to the program, you don’t have a program. And so through the way we did Acorn, it engaged kids and had them show up in the sense of coming back and back and back.”

In 2020, the California State Assembly’s Select Committee on Native American Affairs conferred the honor of a plaque, letter, and on-site visit recognizing the organization’s work to improve and stabilize the lives of Native youth and families in Northern California. The program’s success has attracted interest from other Native Nations seeking to replicate the model. Moorehead said he’s in early conversations with one tribe planning to launch their own version next year, though he declined to name specific nations in preliminary stages.

Another member of the Two Feathers staff, Jayla, who asked to be identified by first name only to protect her privacy, joined the organization at age 15 after seeing an employment ad. A year into her time at Two Feathers, in 2025, President Donald Trump proposed consolidating behavioral health funding. Despite the fact that Trump’s proposal has only been partially implemented, Jayla still sees the impact of it firsthand …

author: Kerry Smith
title: Socialist Alliance: Funding cuts to Villamanta throw people with disability on scrap heap
content:
Brenden Grull, Socialist Alliance spokesperson and candidate for Geelong, has called for funding cuts to Villamanta, Geelong’s Disability Rights Legal Service, to be reversed.

The community-based service, which is housed in Geelong West but works across Victoria, fights for the rights of people with disability-related justice issues. It has been operating since 1990.

The Department of Health and Ageing said on November 10 that it would be cutting approximately 30% of Villamanta’s total funding and around 50% of its core funding.

“It is almost unbelievable that as the demand for disability advocacy increases and in defiance of the Disability Royal Commission’s recommendations to recognise independent advocacy as a vital safeguard for people with disability that Villamanta’s funds are being cut so significantly,” Grull told Green Left.

“I understand that the decision will have an immediate impact; it will lead to substantial job losses. I presume that this is part of the federal government’s cuts to NDIS services.

“It is particularly shocking when independent reviews have recognised that Villamanta is a leader in best-practice disability advocacy and community legal support.”

Grull said the cuts will “only cause more pain and suffering for clients and workers”. He said as cost of living pressures rise for everyone, these cuts show federal Labor’s “diminishing commitment” to community-based organisations.

“Labor’s preference is for dodgy providers from the private sector.”

Grull said Socialist Alliance backs Villamanta’s campaign to get the funding cuts reversed and to protect access to independent disability advocacy.

“We support the reintroduction of publicly-funded disability services to fix gaps in the National Disability Insurance Scheme. Villamanta has our 100% support and we will be doing everything in our power to help restore its funding.”

title: « L'émeute court plus vite que l'aliénation »
content:
Sommes-nous dans une situation pré-autoritaire ou pré-révolutionnaire ? L'insurrection est-elle un devoir en plus d'être un droit ? Faut-il articuler l'émeute au moment électoral ou pas du tout ? Nous nous posons ces questions avec Tristan Garcia (L'autorité est un chantage, 2026) et Patrice Maniglier (La terre ou le monde. Divergences cosmopolitiques. Avec Étienne Balibar. 2025).


À voir lundi 9 novembre :


Quand Marc Crépon affirme sur

C politique

 que l'incendie de la Mairie de Limoges le 17 octobre 2026 relève d'une « ivresse de la destruction » qui – d'une manière honnêtement

boomer

 – évoque pour lui la tarte à la crème du nihilisme des

Possédés

 de Dostoïevski, il ne se rend peut-être pas compte de l'hilarité universelle qu'il suscite chez à peu près tout le monde. Lorsque l'historien, professeur au collège de France, Patrick Boucheron, dans un entretien de Libération, le 31 octobre : dénonce ceux qui continuent de

« croire que la violence émeutière est toujours émancipatrice »

 et pose le constat que nous sommes en situation pré-autoritaire et pas prérévolutionnaire. Il ne se doute pas que nous rions tout autant.


Lundimatin

 n'a que faire des tautologies nihilistes et des dissociations sociales-démocrates. Notre position a toujours été celle de l'

Encyclopédie des émeutes

 : « Ce qui est intéressant dans l'émeute n'est pas une cause, mais un possible » (BE, II, 54). « Toute tentative des pauvres modernes pour organiser le débat sur le monde commence par une émeute : 1789, 1848, 1871, 1917, 1968, et en 1978 en Iran et au Nicaragua. » (BE, II, 55) C'est pourquoi l'émeute est pour nous « le début possible de la fin du monde » (55) et, en général, « un début de débat » sur cette fin (55). Toute émeute ne conduit pas à une insurrection ou une révolution, mais « il n'y a pas de révolution ni d'insurrection qui ne commencent par une émeute. » (55).

author: Chiara Joos
title: Das Recht auf sexuelle Selbstbestimmung
content:
Zwangssterilisation ist verboten. Dennoch erfahren Frauen mit Behinderungen häufig Druck von Angehörigen, Ärzt*innen oder Betreuer*innen, sich sterilisieren zu lassen.

Weißt du, wie viele Menschen ich begleitet habe, die darunter gelitten haben, dass sie sterilisiert wurden?“, fragte mich eine Beraterin am Telefon. Sie schult Menschen mit Behinderungen in Selbstbestimmung. Es war eines von hundert Gesprächen, die meine Kollegin Ramona Arzberger und ich geführt haben, um zur Verhütungspraxis bei Menschen mit Behinderungen zu recherchieren. Nach fast einem Jahr ist daraus der Film „Hauptsache, du kriegst kein Kind“ unseres Magazins „andererseits“ entstanden. Er begleitet mehrere Frauen in Deutschland und Österreich, die mit Lernschwierigkeiten leben und auf Unterstützung angewiesen sind. Drei von ihnen sind sterilisiert. Keine entschied allein. Elf Prozent der Frauen in deutschen Einrichtungen geben an, sterilisiert zu sein, so der Forschungsbericht zu Gewalt und Gewaltschutz in Einrichtungen der Behindertenhilfe des deutschen Bundesministeriums für Arbeit und Soziales von 2024. In Österreich waren es zuletzt 17 Prozent. In Deutschland habe fast die Hälfte der Betroffenen den Eingriff nicht von sich aus gewollt, heißt es in dem Bericht. In Österreich taucht in Befragungen dasselbe auf: Eltern, Ärzt*innen und Betreuer*innen hätten auf die Frauen eingewirkt. „Ich will auch mitmachen!“, platzte die Stimme von Hannelore Trtil ins Telefon, noch ehe meine Kollegin erfuhr, wer da sprach. Die 66-Jährige hatte unseren Flyer gesehen, der Betroffene erreichen sollte. In den 1980er-Jahren wurde sie in Wien „unterbunden“, ein anderes Wort für sterilisiert. „Die haben alle gesagt, man darf keine Kinder kriegen. Das habe ich nicht richtig gefunden. Und das habe ich nicht gewollt“, sagt sie im Film. Heute verbringt sie oft Zeit mit Kindern. Ihre OP-Akte hat das Krankenhaus vor etwa zehn Jahren vernichtet, nach Ablauf der Frist für Schadenersatz. Sie wird nie erfahren, welche Art von Sterilisation bei ihr gemacht wurde. Hannelore sagt auch, sie habe nie Sex gehabt, aus dem ein Kind hätte entstehen können. Diesen Satz haben wir in unseren Recherchen nicht nur von ihr gehört. Thea, die in Wirklichkeit anders heißt, wurde 2025 sterilisiert, in einem Alter, in dem manche noch nicht an Kinder denken. Sie auch nicht. „Weil für uns schon klar war: Das lassen wir.“ Gemeint sind sie und ihre Mutter. Das Wohnhei…Teile diesen Artikel

author: Tam Saavedra
title: WEI and UN Women Co-Launches Guide for Disability-Inclusive
content:
Across Asia and the Pacific, 350 million women and girls with disabilities navigate conflict, crisis, and climate instability. While they are frontline peacebuilders, community leaders, and human rights defenders, they remain systematically excluded from formal peace and security decision-making.

To break down these barriers, Women Enabled International (WEI) and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific have officially launched a landmark publication today: the Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive National Action Plans on Women, Peace and Security in Asia and the Pacific. Released ahead of the annual UN Security Council high-level debate in New York, this first-of-its-kind guide provides a practical, policy-oriented blueprint for governments, policymakers, and civil society.

Read the full Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive NAPs on WPS in Asia and the Pacific

Historically, women with disabilities in peace policies have been viewed narrowly as victims or passive recipients of protection. Co-drafted through consultations with 26 women and gender-diverse people with disabilities, in collaboration with Women Enabled International and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, this guide directly challenges that narrative. It grounds its framework in a human rights model of disability and the core movement principle: “Nothing about us without us”.

As WEI Executive Director Maryangel García-Ramos Guadiana stated during the launch:

“The true value of this Guidance Note is that it exists, not as a siloed document, but as a means to ensure we, as feminist disabled change-makers, are not left out of the agenda, but we are the ones who get to set the agenda.”

UN Women Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific, Christine Arab, added:

“National Action Plans on WPS that include everyone lead to peace that lasts.”

The publication was shaped by participatory research, drawing on focus groups and surveys with 26 grassroots leaders with diverse disabilities across the region. It addresses critical ground-level hurdles—including digital exclusion, inaccessible evacuation infrastructure, and ableism in mainstream spaces—ensuring that the voices of women, girls and gender-diverse people with disabilities form the foundation of the guidance.

The publication urges stakeholders to align National Action Plans (NAPs) with international standards—including the CRPD, CEDAW, and UN Security Council Resolution 2475—across all four WPS pillars:

Participation: Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support.

Participation: Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support.

Prevention: Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators.

Prevention: Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators.

Protection: Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures.

Protection: Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures.

Relief & Recovery: Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities.

Relief & Recovery: Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities.

The guide also features a practical Disability-Inclusive WPS NAP Checklist to help stakeholders evaluate progress at every stage of policy implementation.

This Guidance Note was made possible with the generous support of the Government of the Republic of Korea (through the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family) as part of the project “Promoting Leadership of Future Generation Peacebuilders and Change-makers in Asia and the Pacific”, and of the Australian Government under the Regional Framework Towards Peaceful, Inclusive Societies (2023–2027).

author: James Moore
title: Be More Human: Why Mental Health Care is Broken and What We Can Do to Fix It: An Interview with Sir Norman Lamb
content:
Hello, this is James and welcome to the Mad in America podcast. This week, we are asking why people with mental health conditions die 15-20 years earlier than people without. Why does the UK spend £100 million every year placing patients far from home? How did the question, ‘What matters to you?’ transform mental health care in Norway? Can mental healthcare be more compassionate?

Sir Norman Lamb asks these questions, and more, in his book Be More Human, published by Jessica Kingsley Publishers. Sir Norman is a former Health Minister, an NHS trust chair, and a dedicated mental health campaigner who was knighted in 2019 for his public and political service. He has seen the cracks in the system up close. In his book, he sets out to answer these questions, and many others, uncovering the reasons why our mental health services are failing. He shares eye-opening stories from patients who have been let down, but also inspiring tales from trailblazers who are shaking things up with creative, community-first solutions.

In this interview, we talk about how his personal and professional experiences led to him wanting to lift the lid on the UK’s mental health system. We also discuss how personal accounts of mistreatment and abuse motivated him to think differently about the human element so often missing from mental healthcare. Finally, we discuss novel, community-based alternatives that offer dignity, compassion and hope.

The transcript below has been edited for length and clarity. Listen to the audio of the interview here.

Norman Lamb: Thank you, James. You can drop the Sir bit. I’m happy just to be Norman, but it’s really good to talk to you; great that we’ve got this opportunity.

Lamb: Yes, it’s been an interesting journey, James, because if you scroll back to the late ’90s, early 2000s, I hadn’t really focused much on mental health. It hadn’t touched me in any particular way. Then I was elected to parliament in 2001, and as a member of parliament in North Norfolk, I wanted to be available to constituents to take up their concerns. I became aware of a lot of people coming to see me with their own stories about the mental health system and how, in their terms, they felt it was failing them in various ways: awful waiting lists, awful use of coercion and institutionalisation. Those stories leave a mark on you.

Then we were hit personally in our own family. Our oldest son, Archie, when he was 15, was diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder. We managed to get a referral to the Mental Health Trust at a moment when we were fairly desperate. He was in quite a bad way, and we were told that we would have to wait up to six months for anything to happen.

When you’re a family in despair and really anxious about a child, being told you’ve got to wait up to six months is sort of hopeless, really. I’m acutely conscious that for many people nowadays, it could be a year waiting. We did what any family would do if they’re able to. We paid for care, and in a way, there’s the injustice because most people can’t do that. They are literally just left waiting.

I sort of concluded that a service that leaves people waiting so long when they’re desperate is not really a service at all in any meaningful sense, and everyone preaches the importance of early intervention in mental health. Yet the system seemed to be delivering intervention at the latest possible moment, often when people were already in crisis.

Then scroll forward to 2012: I became a minister in the Department of Health, and you get a whole lot more stories, people coming to talk to you, wanting to influence you, and it’s a profound privilege for people to be willing to tell you their very personal stories. Sometimes about dreadful loss through suicide, but often just other failings of a system that is under acute strain, but failing too many people.

I left the department in 2015, after the General Election that year, and a couple of months after that, my elder sister, Catherine, who’d been in a state of acute depression after the death of our mother, made one or two attempts on her life and was admitted to a fairly dismal unit up in the north of England. She was in there for about 10 weeks. She was a voluntary patient. But despite being a voluntary patient, she was locked up with everybody else.

After her period in there, she was discharged back home. But some months later, she ended up taking her own life, and so our family had to cope with that tragedy, leaving two …

author: dev
title: La menace de l'auto-justice
content:
Au lendemain du 17 octobre, le garde des sceaux Gérald Darmanin, brandie le menace de milices d'auto-défense : « si la réponse pénale aux violences liées au 17 octobre n'est pas extrêmement ferme », alors « les commerçants et les habitants feront justice eux-mêmes ». Une semaine plus tard, le 24, des milices fascistes sous-couvert de défense des petits commerçants attaquent des manifestations dans plusieurs villes de France. De nombreuses vidéos diffusées sur les réseaux sociaux attestent d'une collusion voir d'une collaboration avec les forces de l'ordre. content:
Auteur·e

: Agustín Guillamón

Titre

: Les comités de défense de la CNT à Barcelone (1933-1938)

Date

: 2017


 Tampon du Comité de Défense Local de Barcelone


LES COMITÉS DE DÉFENSE DE LA CNT À BARCELONE (1933-1938)


 Des Cadres de Défense aux Comités révolutionnaires de Quartier, aux Patrouilles de contrôle et aux Milices Populaires


AGUSTÍN GUILLAMÓN


 Première édition en espagnol : avril 2011. Seconde édition en espagnol : septembre 2011. Aldarull edicions. Barcelone.


 Ce livre a été traduit par le Collectif Anarchiste de Traduction et de Scannérisation (CATS) de Caen (et d’ailleurs) en avril et mai 2012, avec le concours précieux de l’auteur. Merci à S. de “La Bataille Socialiste” (

http://bataillesocialiste.wordpress.com/

) pour la mise en relation avec l’auteur. D’autres traductions subversives du CATS sont librement téléchargeables et diffusables sur son site :

http://ablogm.com/cats/


 Un premier brouillon initial (très bref) de ce travail fut publié dans le numéro extraordinaire de Solidaridad Obrera (janvier 2010) dédié au centenaire de la CNT.


 Plus de dirigeants, plus d’État Pour profiter de nos combats.


 — Raoul Vaneigem, La vie s’écoule, la vie s’enfuit


 Vivere militare est.


 — Sénèque. Lettres


 I didn’t say it would be easy, Neo. I just said it would be the truth.


 — Morpheus dans Matrix, Larry et Andy Wachowski.


 « Les révolutions sociales, ces tentatives de réorganisation de la production et de la société sur des nouvelles bases, sont extrêmement rares dans l’Histoire. Au delà des circonstances particulières dans lesquelles elles surgirent, elles nous apportent toujours une expérience irremplaçable, dans leurs succès comme, surtout, dans leurs échecs. Le grand enseignement de la révolution de 1936 a été la nécessité incontournable de la destruction de l’État ».


 Barricade construite le 19 Juillet 1936 sur le Paralelo, face à « El Molino ». Ici les Comités de Défense et le Syndicat du Bois de la CNT mirent en déroute l’armée soulevée.


1. DU RAPPORT DE SHAPIRO À CELUI D’OCTOBRE 1934


 Un rapport confidentiel, à la diffusion réduite, d’Alexandre Shapiro

[1]

, secrétaire de l’AIT, élaboré durant son séjour en Espagne en 1932-33, relatait ce qu’étaient et comment fonctionnaient les Comités de Défense, organisés exclusivement pour des tâches insurrectionnelles de choc, comme celle du 8 janvier 1933, dont il fut témoin. Ce rapport de Shapiro, sur les Comités de Défense, fut réalisé en pleine polémique entre FAIstes et trentistes

[2]

 sur l’opportunité, ou non, de la tactique d’insurrection immédiate, localiste et permanente. Shapiro fit une critique dévastatrice de l’improvisation, du manque d’organisation et de préparation de l’insurrection de janvier. Il dénonça, avec dureté, le fait qu’une même personne puisse détenir des charges aux secrétariats de la CNT et du Comité National de Défense, pour le confusionnisme que cela créait. Il démontra que, dans la pratique, s’était produite une soumission de la CNT aux décisions du Comité National des Comités de Défense (CNDC).


 Le rapport de Shapiro, qui bénéficiait de l’aide inestimable d’Eusebio Carbó, décrivait de cette manière les Cadres de Défense, existants en 1933 : « Ces Comités de Défense, qui existaient déjà depuis un certain temps, avaient comme unique but de préparer les armes nécessaires en cas d’insurrection, d’organiser les groupes de choc dans les différents quartiers populaires, d’organiser la résistance des soldats dans les casernes etc… ».


 Alors même que l’insurrection des Asturies était encore en cours, le CNCD constatait, dans un rapport

[3]

, l’échec de la tactique insurrectionnelle, défendue par le groupe Nosotros, connue populairement sous le nom de « gymnastique révolutionnaire », qu’il accusait précisément d’être responsable du manque de préparation de la CNT pour intervenir, au niveau national, dans l’insurrection d’octobre 1934. Le moment était venu de dépasser cette tactique, parce qu’elle avait démontré le caractère absurde et dangereux d’une insurrection locale à un moment inadéquat, sans une sérieuse préparation préalable, qui soumettait les libertaires à la répression étatique, sans jamais obtenir une extension populaire à tout le pays, ni l’adhésion des autres organisations, nécessaire pour affronter avec succès l’appareil militaire et répressif de l’État. Le pire de tout est que cette répression avait démantelé l’appareil militaire clandestin de la CNT, après les insurrections …

В маленькой редакционной комнате еженедельной пропагандистской газеты мы с наслаждением предавались дружеской беседе между товарищами, как вдруг вошёл рослый парень с ремнём за плечами.

Он весело поздоровался с присутствующими, расстегнул ремни, поставил ящик на пол и сел на него, вытирая пот.

Пока мы ждали, что он заговорит, мы молча рассматривали его. Это был высокий, широкоплечий юноша с чёрными усиками на смуглой, загорелой коже и живыми, искрящимися глазами, как пенистое вино. Одет он был в деревенскую одежду, с некоторыми городскими штрихами или отголосками города.

Наконец, с улыбкой, очень непринуждённо, гость назвал своё имя.

Администратор газеты прекрасно знал его как неутомимого активиста, который очень часто писал ему – то из одного населённого пункта, то из другого – и с дьявольской энергией распространял брошюры. Где бы он ни проходил, люди массами подписывались на газету. Если он не был коммивояжёром, то уж точно был Вечным жидом[1]… – Вечным жидом пропаганды, – сказал парень с ящиком, широко и довольно улыбаясь.

И поскольку на наших лицах откровенно разливалась жадная любопытность, он принялся в общих чертах рассказывать о своей кочевой жизни.

В городе он был механиком и уже зарабатывал хорошую зарплату. Но, будучи человеком читающим и стремящимся к знаниям, завсегдатаем собраний, жадно ловившим каждое слово из дискуссий, которые велись в помещении профсоюза, он вскоре воспламенился нашим прекрасным идеалом человеческого освобождения. И тут же его охватила ненасытная жажда обращать в свою веру, тут же его озаботила великая проблема сельской пропаганды, сеяния за пределами промышленных центров – по этим обширным невозделанным полям провинции, тревожным и полным тайны. Далеко ли может зайти любая попытка городского рабочего, одинокого и встречающего враждебность? Почему бы не последовать прекрасному примеру русских революционеров, которые идут жить и работать среди крестьян?

Молодой и крепкий, без семейных обязательств, в один прекрасный день наш парень отправился по этим землям. Он запасся полезными и дешёвыми предметами, которые продавал с минимальной прибылью. Он изучил основы различных ремёсел и был на селе услужливым умельцем на все руки. В деревенских хижинах не было мебели или утвари, которую он не сумел бы починить или даже изготовить. Он даже чинил грубую обувь, за неимением сапожника, и нередко видели, как он вносил свой изобретательный вклад в ремонт или строительство домов…

При этом он довольствовался малым. Есть и спать – как придётся: иногда лучше, иногда хуже; иногда за несколько грошей, иногда в уплату за работу. В жаркое время он не брезговал спать под открытым небом, на гумнах или под скирдами. Умирать – не умирал. В общем: жил помаленьку – и со здоровьицем…

Таким образом он быстро завоёвывал сердца и доверие людей из деревень и маленьких городков, которые внимательно слушали его беседы и публичные чтения, охотно принимали его брошюры и газеты, задумчиво следили за ясными и светлыми картинами будущего, будущего с большей свободой и большим довольством.

Мы с волнением смотрели на доброго сеятеля, запоминая его облик и черты, словно пытаясь увидеть воплощение той благороднейшей страсти и того животворящего героизма.

— Вот уже пять лет веду эту жизнь, – просто заключил он.

Мы предположили, что он имеет в виду холеру и месть властей. Нет; мы поняли неправильно: речь шла об узах любви. Случаев и соблазнов ему не хватало; и не то чтобы он хвастался, но о многих он знал, что они не сказали бы ему «нет»… Но, честно говоря, решение не казалось ему из самых лёгких, как и не находил он лёгким найти женщину, которая бы ему подошла. Ужасная проблема…

И когда доблестный парень собрался уходить, уже приготовив свой запас печатной …

content:
