author: Unknown
title: Michel Kokoreff: We are witnessing the political awakening of a generation in France
content:
The protests initiated by high school and university students in France have gone beyond problems within the education system, evolving into a broader social movement against social inequalities, neoliberal policies and the State's increasingly repressive measures.


Police interventions against student demonstrations have intensified debates in the country concerning democratic rights and freedoms. Meanwhile, the rise of the far right across Europe and the crisis facing capitalism have also become major issues on the political agenda.


French sociologist Professor Michel Kokoreff, who teaches at Paris 8 University, spoke to ANF about the student protests in France, police violence, the social consequences of neoliberal policies and the rise of the far right in Europe.


For several weeks, high school and university students have been mobilising in France. Beyond demands related to education, what do these mobilisations reveal about the social and political tensions currently affecting French society?


It's always difficult to answer because the movement is still ongoing, so inevitably, this is a somewhat immediate analysis. However, it is nevertheless informed by, as you rightly mentioned, around ten different studies, since France has been shaken for roughly ten years by a number of social movements that have been somewhat unprecedented in their format, composition and political consequences.


What this reveals, in my view, above all, is the political awakening of a generation. The generational awakening of high school students from working-class backgrounds, who attend schools in peripheral areas. For example, in the Paris region, in the department of Seine-Saint-Denis, what is sometimes called the

peripheral school system

: that is, a school system that is much less well-funded than schools located within the city limits of Paris. And this awakening has manifested itself through a rather explosive mixture of joy and anger.


Joy has been expressed, in particular, through the many banners and placards that appeared during demonstrations. They were often very inventive, often remarkably perceptive, full of irony.  At the same time, there has been anger regarding teaching conditions, their deterioration, the shortage of teachers, the extremely high temperatures in summer and the freezing conditions in winter due to a lack of proper equipment. In doing so, these young people have taken up a number of demands that trade unions have been putting forward for around ten years, particularly following the reform of the so-called Blanquer baccalaureate in 2018. These demands had not been heard, but this time they have benefited from considerably greater visibility. And this combination of joy, this cocktail of joy, anger and determination, expressed through blockades, particularly of a number of high schools, and these confrontational actions, has gone viral on social media.


We therefore saw university students initially joining the movement, so to speak, with their own demands, but also out of solidarity. Other sectors of French society and the world of work followed, particularly in the public sector, but not exclusively. Gradually, and we will undoubtedly come back to this, this high school and university student movement became a societal movement, perhaps more than a social movement in the traditional sense of one organised by trade unions. It triggered a political crisis at the highest level of the State. This was due, firstly, to the absence of any response for 15 days, the silence of the ministers responsible, namely the Minister of National Education and the Minister of Higher Education. There was no response; there was silence for 15 days. Fifteen days is a long time. And above all, there was what the Minister of the Interior described as repression carried out "without restraint" by law enforcement agencies and the police. There were no instructions to show restraint towards these young minors, many of whom were just 14 or 15 years old.


This resulted in brutal interventions, mutilations, hands being torn off, people losing an eye, and, more generally, people being traumatised. Obviously, a number of images also went viral on social media. These images provided an indication of the movement itself, but also exposed the brutality of police interventions. In a way, we could also speak of the cynicism of politicians, both men and women, who justified this police violence in the name of fighting urban …

title: Social siege in Yüksekova: Children, women and youth targeted - Part Two
content:
Allegations of child sexual abuse, harassment and sexual assault against women in Hakkari (Colemêrg), particularly in Yüksekova (Gever), have brought long-standing social problems in the district back into focus. 


The first part of this feature can be read

here

.  


The sexual assault cases involving the names of Necat Koparan, Eren Oğuz and Nevzat Çiftçi reveal a situation that society in Yüksekova (Gever) can no longer ignore. Necat Koparan and Eren Oğuz are named in the case involving the alleged sexual assault of a 13-year-old child, based on the child's testimony. Koparan is a wedding musician and also a security guard. Oğuz is a school bus driver. Several women have also made allegations of sexual assault, harassment, threats and blackmail against wedding musician Nevzat Çiftçi.


The fact that these individuals continue to perform at weddings raises serious questions for society. If reports that Eren Oğuz is still transporting students are accurate, how should families who entrust their children to school buses respond to this situation?


Why, then, are these two wedding musicians still invited to perform at weddings despite the allegations of sexual assault, harassment and other incidents surrounding them and the network of troubling relationships in which their names appear? Do wedding hosts, families and organizers never ask themselves: "Have you no shame? On what grounds are you inviting these individuals to your weddings?" How can it be considered normal for them to continue performing as though nothing has happened when such serious allegations have been made?


Kurdish weddings are gatherings that bring together families, relatives, neighbors and local communities, with their own distinctive social bonds. Families organize the weddings, and people from villages and neighborhoods attend. Why, then, is there not greater scrutiny when these individuals are invited to perform? Why do families, relatives, shopkeepers, local politicians and respected community figures not respond more strongly? Are a few press statements and messages of condemnation enough?


Another issue raised in videos and during our interviews concerns the presence of soldiers and police officers at neighborhood weddings, particularly around these two wedding musicians. What are specialist sergeants and police officers doing at Kurdish weddings where families, relatives and neighbors gather? How do they attend these events? Through whom do they establish connections with these circles? What is the nature of their relationships? Why are these environments, where women and children have reported harassment and sexual assault, not being questioned?


Another important question is why society's own mechanisms of accountability are not being activated. What position are families, villages, neighborhoods, shopkeepers, local politicians and respected community figures taking in response to these incidents? Why are individuals facing such serious allegations still invited to weddings? Is no one willing to question their continued performances?


Destroyed neighborhoods and a new social siege


The collapse of the resolution process and the intensification of clashes after 2015 brought many cities across Kurdistan under siege in every aspect of life. Treating developments in Hakkari (Colemêrg) and its districts, particularly Yüksekova, as isolated incidents prevents us from understanding the broader picture. The destruction of neighborhoods during urban clashes cannot be viewed merely as a consequence of armed conflict. We must also recognize that neighborhood culture and collective memory were targeted through this destruction.


The new buildings constructed in place of demolished neighborhoods, together with the unfamiliar way of life introduced into the town, were intended to sever people's connections with their culture and roots. This was not simply a matter of constructing new buildings. It was an intervention in the shared culture of a town, relations between neighbors, neighborhood solidarity and society's collective capacity to respond. Displacing people from their living spaces and forcing them into a different way of life was also part of this policy.


How, then, was this siege carried out? As clashes intensified during the period of self-rule, local political representation, broader political structures, the press, local cultural solidarity networks and all organized structures within society were targeted. These structures …

title: One family, six comrades
content:
Kurdish movements advocating the freedom of the Kurdish people and Kurdistan have been established in their dozens, from the period when the existence of the Kurds and Kurdistan was denied to the present day. Some of these movements carried out armed and political struggles for decades, while others disintegrated in their early years as a result of plots by their enemies. Many movements were established, but many were also eliminated. These movements carried out their activities through the love that the people of Kurdistan held in their hearts. Numerous young people sacrificed their lives for their objectives. Many Kurdish youths were tortured, imprisoned and killed for the same cause. Their fundamental aim was to struggle for a free Kurdistan. Thousands followed in their footsteps and embraced the ideology of Kurdistan's freedom. Among them were many people with distinctive and remarkable stories.


This article tells the life stories of comrades Nîştîman and Mezlûm and how they joined the struggle. Mezlûm and Nîştîman were life partners and comrades in struggle. They had two children and came from Mûçêj, a town in Kamyaran in Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat). They lived with strong patriotic convictions and devoted themselves to the struggle. Both had worked within organisations in Eastern Kurdistan and made sacrifices for their political activities.


 


Mezlûm Viyan described his disillusionment with Kurdish political movements and how he later became acquainted with the ideas of Abdullah Öcalan. He said: “My name is Mezlûm Viyan. I was born in Mûçêj, Kamyaran. Comrade Nîştîman and I had established a garden where we grew tomatoes. We had created a vegetable garden and dug a well there. One evening, while walking towards the village, I saw Öcalan's name written on the walls.


I had previously worked in other political movements. I was active in the Tudeh Party and later joined the Komala Party. I carried out political activities in Sine. Because of my activities, I also spent two years in Iranian prisons. However, these traditional parties betrayed the people. The good people among them were martyred. Others took control of these parties through conspiracies. After Kak Fuad was martyred, a family from Bokan took control of the Komala Party. This family put its own interests first and forgot the people. After witnessing all this, I came to hate politics. I would not allow anyone in our home to talk about politics because the people had been betrayed. Villagers had shared their food with them and opened their doors to them. Yet they went and surrendered, exposing our people to arrest. Many people were imprisoned as a result. From that day onwards, I hated politics. I would not allow anyone to discuss politics in my presence.”


Baz becomes the first to join the Freedom Movement


Mezlûm Viyan said that he embraced Abdullah Öcalan's ideas after reading his books. He said: “At one point, a cadre from the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) came to our home. I was told that he was a university student. That was how he was introduced to me. Later, one day at the university, I asked my son Baz, ‘Who is this Öcalan?’ He replied, ‘Would you like me to bring you his books?’ I said, ‘Bring them.’ He brought me the book How to Live. From its opening pages, I realised how different this leader's political definitions and ideas about building society were from those of Marx, Engels, Mao, Che Guevara, and even the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad Mustafa and all the books in the world. I do not know why, but my heart was racing as I read that book. The moment I sat beside the water pool and read it, I fell in love with that leader. As I read, I understood that his perspective on building society was different from other perspectives. I saw no personal interest in these ideas. That was why I fell in love with them.”


After becoming acquainted with the movement, Mezlûm's son Baz left his family and joined its ranks. Baz's decision marked the beginning of a remarkable story of patriotism for the family. Mezlûm Viyan said that Baz had travelled to the Qandil mountains, where he received ten days of training before returning to complete his university education. He recalled: “After university, Baz said, ‘I am going to join the movement.’ Baz was the first among us to join. After Baz joined, Nîştîman told me, ‘Go and ask about our son. Find out where he is and what he is doing.’ I left Eastern Kurdistan and travelled to Southern …

author: Unknown
title: The Republic’s second century: Whose future?
content:
As the Republic of Turkey enters its second century, it is seeking to redefine not only its past but also its future. Amid shifting balances in the Middle East, new alliances and regional power struggles, Turkey is searching for ways to adapt the continuity of the state to new circumstances. The Kurdish question is once again being placed at the centre of this search.


However, there is a historical distinction that must not be overlooked: the Republic's attempt to reshape its own future is not the same as the Kurds determining their own future.


Today, a new political language is being constructed around concepts such as “brotherhood”, “the domestic front”, “common destiny”, “democratic integration”, “a terror-free Turkey” and “a terror-free region”. Each of these concepts can carry different meanings. Yet political language does not merely describe reality; it also determines which demands are considered legitimate and which futures are regarded as possible. As this new semantic space is constructed, the aim is not only to reshape political language but also to redefine which demands are considered legitimate and which futures are deemed possible.


The founding period of the Republic and its historical context cannot be excluded from today's debate. Stefan Ihrig, a professor of history at the University of Haifa who has researched the influence of the founding of modern Turkey on German political thought, demonstrates in his book Atatürk in the Nazi Imagination how the nationalist movement led by Mustafa Kemal was followed, discussed and taken as a model by the German far right and emerging Nazi circles, drawing on publications from the period.


One striking example of this influence was the demand for an “Ankara government” in Germany, expressed in publications associated with the Nazi movement in 1923. These findings do not equate the two regimes. However, they show how the founding of the Republic was interpreted in European fascist circles as a model for overcoming defeat, national reconstruction and strong centralised power. This represents a historical dimension outside the official founding narrative that cannot be ignored.


The significance of Ihrig's research for today's debate lies not in establishing a direct parallel between the past and the present, but in demonstrating that processes of state formation cannot be understood solely through their own narratives of legitimacy. The founding of the Republic held different meanings for different political circles. Similarly, the “Turkey model” being brought back onto the agenda today cannot be assessed solely through the concepts used by its advocates. What matters is whether this model recognises the Kurds as equal political subjects capable of determining their own future, or whether it places their future within boundaries redefined by the state.


This question had a concrete significance for the Kurds during the founding period of the Republic. The research of Ismail Beşikçi and historical studies of the Koçgiri Rebellion reveal the conflict between Kurdish demands for political status and autonomy and Ankara's conception of centralised sovereignty even before the Republic was proclaimed. The events in Koçgiri in 1920 and 1921 brought into focus the question of who would be recognised as a founding political subject of the new state. Would the Kurds become political partners in this order, or would their existence be defined within boundaries determined by the state?


Behind this question lay continuities carried over from the final period of the Ottoman Empire into the Republic. The demographic and property arrangements that emerged following the Armenian Genocide of 1915, together with the continuity of certain administrative and political cadres, demonstrate that 1923 did not represent a complete break with the past. The Republic did not merely establish new institutions; it also made national homogenisation one of the fundamental instruments of state formation. The tension between this approach and democracy was not directed solely against the Kurds. The single-party system, the authoritarian turn of the Democrat Party and the military coup of 27 May also demonstrate the Republic's troubled relationship with political pluralism. For the Kurds, however, the issue was more fundamental: restrictions on democratic rights were accompanied by the denial of a people's collective existence and political future. Denial would become institutionalised …

author: Unknown
title: Peoples’ Climate Summit calls for a democratic energy transition
content:
The Peoples’ Climate Summit in Antalya continued its discussions on the second day with a fundamental critique of global energy policy. During a three-part event titled “Phasing Out Fossil Fuels and Energy Democracy,” representatives of international climate movements, trade unions and environmental initiatives discussed alternatives to an energy system dominated by fossil fuels and the interests of major corporations.


The summit is being held as an alternative event to the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31). While the official negotiations focus on international climate policy, participants at the alternative summit emphasized the social consequences of the climate crisis, the historical responsibility of industrialized countries and the right of affected communities to participate in decision-making.


“It is not about charity, but justice”


Opening the session, Leon Sealey-Huggins of the British organization War on Want criticized the growing concentration of economic and political power. He argued that the current environmental and social crises were not accidental developments, but consequences of an economic system that prioritized the interests of a privileged few over the needs of the majority. Those particularly affected, he said, included low-income communities, small-scale farmers and people whose livelihoods were threatened by environmental destruction and rising energy prices.


Sealey-Huggins warned against reducing the energy transition to the electrification of consumption in the Global North. “While increasing amounts of energy are being supplied to electric cars, air conditioning systems and data centers, around 700 million people worldwide still lack access to basic electricity. A just transition must therefore prioritize the needs of the people.”


Sealey-Huggins also highlighted the colonial history of economic inequality. He noted that the Global North had benefited for centuries from the extraction of raw materials and labor from colonized societies, arguing that these historical relationships must also be taken into account when financing the energy transition.


“It is not about charity, but justice. It is about redistributing wealth and power,” Sealey-Huggins stated. He called for a global Green New Deal that would have to be achieved through the collective struggle of trade unions, feminist movements, Indigenous communities and environmental initiatives.


Climate justice and the rights of Indigenous communities


Rukia Khamis of the international climate organization 350.org emphasized that economic development models from the Global North could not simply be transferred to other societies without taking local conditions into account. She argued that economic growth did not automatically translate into environmentally sustainable development. The historical responsibility of industrialized countries toward the Global South must therefore be a central component of international climate policy, she underlined.


Her colleague João Cerqueira addressed disputes over Indigenous territories in Brazil. Citing the example of the Guarani-Kaiowá people, he described a ruling by a Brazilian federal court prohibiting the issuance of new project permits in the area concerned without prior consultation with Indigenous communities. “A territory does not have to be officially recognized by the state in order to be protected,” Cerqueira explained.


He stressed that Indigenous communities should not merely be consulted on energy projects that had already been approved. Instead, he added, they must have the right to decide for themselves what kinds of economic and environmental development take place on their land. This includes the right to reject new fossil fuel extraction projects.


“In Brazil, in Turkey and everywhere around the world, communities are at the forefront of resistance. Along rivers, in courtrooms and on the streets, they are deciding their own future,” Cerqueira said.


Women bear the social consequences of energy policies


Süheyla Doğan, chair of the Association for the Protection of the Natural and Cultural Heritage of Mount Ida, addressed the gender-specific impacts of the energy crisis. She noted that the coal and energy industries remained heavily male-dominated. Women, she said, were underrepresented both in the workforce and in leadership positions, yet bore a significant share of the social consequences of job losses and workplace accidents.

author: Unknown
title: The silent friendship between guerrillas and mountain goats
content:
When human beings become one with nature, they can understand its language. To achieve this, people must live in nature, care for it and protect it. Those who have come to understand this truth are the freedom guerrillas. That is why they establish their bases on mountaintops where the earth meets the sky. All kinds of plants and animals gather around them.


The mountain goat is one of the animals that inhabit the mountain peaks. It is an extremely alert and sensitive animal that is difficult to capture or tame. Mountain goats do not approach humans unless they are convinced that no harm will come to them.


Guerrillas are known for their commitment to protecting nature. Indeed, one of the fundamental pillars of Abdullah Öcalan’s paradigm is environmental protection. For this reason, guerrillas carry out their struggle and live their lives with this awareness.


Guerrillas take mountain goats into their care for a while, helping them survive. They later release them back into the wild.


https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/a3645ecc_20261113150527_2026-11-15-behdinan-gerilayen-yja-star-hevaltiya-jidil-a-gerila-u-pezkovi-1.mp4


The time spent together also allows a shared language to develop between the guerrillas and the mountain goats. Through this language, a friendship emerges from which everyone can learn something. Indeed, many accounts of guerrilla life describe the friendships they have formed with animals.


This is no ordinary friendship. Because of the sincere bond guerrillas establish with all living beings, nature, in turn, protects, nourishes and shelters them in times of hardship and adversity. This is a relationship of mutual interaction and complementarity between guerrillas and nature.

author: Unknown
title: Yılmaz: Failure to implement ECtHR rulings is a constitutional crime
content:
Turkey's continued refusal to implement rulings issued by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) concerning human rights violations is deepening debates over the rule of law and human rights.


Legal experts point out that the failure to implement ECtHR rulings not only perpetuates individual rights violations but also undermines the principle of the rule of law and public confidence in justice.


Ercan Yılmaz, co-chair of the Amed (Diyarbakır) branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD), spoke to ANF regarding Turkey's non-compliance with ECtHR judgments and the consequences.


https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/22868199_20261111145819_2026-11-12-amed-ercan-yilmaz-ihd-sube-baskani-uygulanmayan-aihm-kararlari-1.mp4


'Failure to implement ECtHR rulings is nothing new'


Ercan Yılmaz recalled that Turkey's failure to implement ECtHR rulings was not a new issue as the problem had long become much more visible, particularly after 2016 and the transition from the parliamentary system to the Presidential Government System in 2017.


Yılmaz stated: "Following the attempted coup in 2016, Turkey introduced a change to its system of government in 2017. The parliamentary system was abandoned and replaced by a presidential system.


Since then, the failure to implement ECtHR rulings has become a much more prominent issue in our lives. In particular, non-compliance with judgments finding violations of the rights of people imprisoned for political reasons, and the continued refusal to carry out release orders, have called into question the position of the ECtHR and the judicial authority that Turkey has recognised.


Particularly in the 1990s, no results were achieved through Turkey's domestic legal system regarding crimes committed against citizens by state forces or paramilitary groups. Once domestic legal remedies had been exhausted, numerous cases and applications were brought before the European Court of Human Rights. The Court issued very serious judgments against Turkey. There are thousands of judgments concerning violations of the right to life, enforced disappearances, the prohibition of torture, and freedom of thought and expression. Even at that time, these judgments were not properly implemented within Turkey's domestic legal system."


'The Demirtaş and Kavala rulings undermined confidence in the law'


Ercan Yılmaz said that the failure to implement ECtHR rulings had become particularly visible through judgments concerning well-known public figures.


He continued: "The non-obedience with the judgments concerning Selahattin Demirtaş and Osman Kavala within domestic law has had serious consequences both for individual citizens and society as a whole. Confidence in the principle of legal certainty, the belief that there are courts people can turn to and seek protection of their rights, has been severely undermined.


The fact that courts act on political motives has existed for a long time. However, this has now become much more visible throughout society because the individuals concerned are well known. Among them are Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ, the former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP), and businessman Osman Kavala, who is also well known among civil society organisations in Turkey. The failure of domestic courts to implement the judgments concerning these cases has also caused serious concerns among ordinary people.


We are facing an approach that has completely destroyed confidence in the law. People are losing faith that courts will protect their rights and remedy unlawful practices. A court finds a violation, yet the judicial institutions of the country responsible for implementing that judgment refuse to do so. This also places serious obstacles in the way of people's pursuit of justice."


'The right to hope ruling has not been implemented for 12 years'


Yılmaz said that the ECtHR's 2014 ruling concerning the "right to hope" for Abdullah Öcalan had not resulted in the necessary legal or practical changes in Turkey.


Yılmaz further stated: "There was a ruling concerning the right to hope in 2014. There are also judgments concerning other prisoners. The judgments concerning Mr. Öcalan and Civan Boltan are among them. However, no changes have been made to Turkey's domestic legal system in the past 12 years.

author: Unknown
title: Kılıç: Villagers are leading the ecological struggle
content:
The growing number of mining, solar power plant (SPP) and hydroelectric power plant (HPP) projects in Kurdistan and Turkey are being pushed forward through favourable Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) decisions. The planned projects threaten pastures and groundwater resources, which are among the main sources of livelihood for villagers in the region. Local people seeking to protect their living spaces and livelihoods continue to organise against these projects across villages and districts.


In the past year alone, eight local platforms have been established in Kurdistan to oppose planned projects, while protest camps have been set up in numerous villages. Varto (Gimgim), Sur, Karlıova (Kanîreş), Kulp (Pasur) and Şırnak (Şirnex) have emerged as prominent centres of ecological resistance. Hundreds of villagers have come together through these platforms to pursue legal action and organise resistance on the ground.


 


Sabri Kılıç, spokesperson for the Amed (Diyarbakır) Ecology Council, who has closely followed and participated in recent protests, said that the social base of the ecological struggle is expanding and that the resistance is generating ecological and social awareness. He said: "It is particularly valuable to see people of all ages, from children to the elderly, coming together to defend their living spaces in villages directly affected by ecological destruction."


166 EIA announcements published


A total of 166 EIA announcements were published in Amed between 1 January and 17 October 2026. Of these, 73 resulted in favourable decisions, while six applications were cancelled or returned. Solar power plant projects also accounted for a significant share of the city's EIA procedures. During this period, announcements were published for 29 SPP projects, eight of which received favourable decisions.


'Companies are exploiting the process'


Kılıç said that ecological destruction in Kurdistan cannot be understood merely as the result of projects undertaken by a handful of companies, describing it instead as a systematic policy of exploitation. He stressed that the issue extends beyond environmental destruction and must be considered in its economic, social, cultural and political dimensions. Kılıç also said that this policy had intensified again following the beginning of the peace process.


Kılıç continued: "Since the Call for Peace and a Democratic Society, we have seen capital, through certain monopolies, develop an increasingly voracious appetite for Kurdistan, attempting to turn every area into a site of capital accumulation. Operating entirely according to a logic of exploitation, they are causing ecological destruction across Kurdistan through mining sites, quarries, oil exploration wells, energy projects and similar activities.


The important point is that these projects are being imposed on village pastures, agricultural land, water resources and forest areas. People who were forced to migrate through the burning and evacuation of villages in the 1990s are now being driven from their homes by capital through a different approach. This also threatens villages' relations of production, livelihoods, collective memory and the cultural and historical ties that people have established with the land they inhabit."


'Villagers have become active agents of resistance'


Kılıç emphasised the importance of the struggle waged by villagers against ecological destruction, saying that they should not be regarded merely as victims. Instead, he stressed that villagers have become social actors who speak for themselves, defend their right to make decisions about their living spaces and develop organised resistance.


Kılıç said: "This growing struggle should be recognised not only as resistance against ecological destruction and an effort to protect living spaces, but also as a valuable contribution to the development of local democracy and social organisation."


'Social awareness against plunder has emerged'


Kılıç also highlighted the continuity of the villagers' struggle. He said: "Based on our observations over the past year, we can say that the social base of the ecological struggle has expanded and that the resistance has generated ecological and social awareness. Furthermore, in villages directly affected by ecological destruction, it is particularly valuable to see people of all ages, from children to the elderly, standing together to defend their living spaces.

author: Unknown
title: Narges Mohammadi calls for solidarity with imprisoned writers
content:
Human rights activist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi issued a statement from prison to mark International Day of the Imprisoned Writer.


Drawing attention to authoritarian governments’ attitudes towards freedom of expression and thought, Narges Mohammadi stated that Iran’s history was also filled with methods of repression ranging from executions and imprisonment to fabricated cases and threats.


Narges Mohammadi said that journalists, writers and poets Arash Galeh-Golab, Mandana Sadeghi, Reza Mohammadi, Kourosh Keram-Pour and Farzaneh Yahya-Abadi were being retried in connection with the same case. She noted that all five had been charged on 9 November by Branch 103 of the Abadan Criminal Court No. 2 with “spreading false news with the aim of misleading public opinion” and “participating in illegal gatherings”.


Narges Mohammadi added that the death sentence handed down to poet and songwriter Peyman Farah-Avar had been referred to the Execution Office. The statement also highlighted the five-year-and-one-month prison sentence imposed on Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi, along with the confiscation of his assets; the detention of Mahshahr-based poet and writer Ilyas Kenavati-Lari; and the four-year-and-eight-month prison sentences handed down to two writers and poets from Gorgan, Ruzbeh Gilasian and Nima Saffar.


Pointing to the difficulty of establishing the exact number of writers and artists who are imprisoned, detained or facing judicial prosecution, Narges Mohammadi stressed the importance of supporting every imprisoned writer.


Narges Mohammadi also cited the PEN Award being presented to two imprisoned Iranian writers, Golrokh Iraee and Ali Asadollahi, as an example of how international support and attention can amplify the voices of prisoners.

author: cnt.es
title: Organizaciones sindicales y sociales de Zamora denuncian las actuaciones policiales durante la huelga general del 11N
content:
Las organizaciones sindicales y sociales convocantes y participantes en la huelga general del 11 de noviembre en Zamora han hecho público un comunicado conjunto en el que valoran positivamente la movilización, agradecen la participación de la ciudadanía y denuncian las actuaciones policiales durante la jornada.


Bajo el lema «La lluvia no nos detuvo. Los golpes tampoco nos detendrán», las organizaciones destacan la respuesta de la clase trabajadora pese a las adversas condiciones meteorológicas. Desde La Marina hasta la Plaza de la Constitución, miles de personas salieron a la calle para defender sus derechos y mostrar que «Zamora no está dispuesta a resignarse».


El comunicado expresa también su solidaridad con las personas agredidas y detenidas durante la jornada y denuncia especialmente lo ocurrido en las cocheras de los autobuses urbanos. Según relatan, la empresa se negó a presentar las hojas de servicios mínimos a los miembros del Comité de Huelga, pese a que la ley establece sus funciones de negociación y vigilancia. Asimismo, denuncian que la policía obstaculizó el trabajo del comité, llegando a producirse agresiones y la detención de dos compañeros.


Las organizaciones convocantes consideran que la actuación policial tuvo como objetivo generar miedo, tensión e inseguridad entre quienes ejercían legítimamente su derecho a la huelga. Advierten de que las cargas, las multas y las detenciones no van a borrar las razones que llevaron a la ciudadanía a movilizarse ni a frenar la defensa de unas condiciones de vida dignas, salarios justos, derechos laborales y justicia social.


El comunicado concluye reafirmando la voluntad de continuar con las movilizaciones y la organización colectiva:

«El 11N no ha sido un punto final. Ha sido un paso más»

.


«¡La lucha continúa! ¡Nos vemos en las calles!»

author: C.
title: Das Ende des Status quo, der Wandel steht bevor (mit unklaren Folgen!)
content:
In einem Artikel, den ich vor etwa anderthalb Jahren geschrieben habe, habe ich folgende Kritik und Analyse zu den linken/aktivistischen Kreisen in Berlin geäußert:


https://kontrapolis.info/14975/


„Die Person kritisiert den Staat, die Gesellschaft oder das System, in dem sie lebt, in Reden und Taten, aber es gibt keine Wut oder einen Bruch in ihren Gefühlen. Denn alles in ihrem Leben ist in Ordnung und läuft mehr oder weniger so, wie sie es will, sie hat erreicht, was sie tun will, sie hat gesehen, was sie sehen will, es gibt keine großen Unterschiede zwischen Ideal und Wirklichkeit. Es gibt Stabilität, Sicherheit und vielfältige Zukunftsperspektiven in ihrem Leben. Obwohl sie in der Rede radikale Kritik und Maßnahmen gegen den deutschen Staat und die deutsche Gesellschaft gutheißen (und redet übrigens oft mehr über ihre „Prekarität“ als die prekärsten Menschen selbst, dass sie den Staat-die Nation-die Gesellschaft am meisten hasst), liegt ihnen der Fortbestand von Ordnung und Status quo am Herzen -wie ich mich fühle, natürlich-.“


Soweit ich das in den letzten 1,5 Jahren beobachten konnte, gab es zwei Entwicklungen – sowohl gute als auch schlechte. Die Welt ist viel unberechenbarer geworden und die Wahrscheinlichkeit, dass sie sich in einen dystopischen Ort verwandelt, ist gestiegen; das ist schlecht, weil es vielleicht Milliarden Menschen betreffen wird – und damit auch uns linke aktivistische Menschen, die in Berlin leben. Aber es ist auch gut, weil der Status-quo-Glaube der linken Kreise und ihre tiefen emotionalen Bindungen an den Staat und das System gebrochen wurden.


Jeden Tag erkennen mehr Menschen, dass der Status quo nicht weiterbestehen wird – und das gilt natürlich nicht nur für linke Kreise, sondern auch für (neo-)maskulinistische, an Ungleichheit glaubende rechte Kreise und natürlich für die schwerfälligen Staaten aus vergangenen Zeiten, die versuchen, sich in einer sich wandelnden und weiter verändernden Welt zu positionieren. In Berliner linken Kreisen gab es schon immer revolutionäre Ideen, aber (fast) keine revolutionären Gefühle – und gerade deshalb war sie nicht einmal von sich selbst überzeugt. Doch jetzt, da diese Gefühle da sind, hat auch die Organisation damit begonnen.


Und der Wandel steht bevor. Wir nähern uns nun dem Moment, in dem wir zu echten Subjekten werden, in dem wir über die uns gegebenen Optionen hinaus Entscheidungen über unser eigenes Leben treffen und diese direkt umsetzen können. Statt uns (nur) zu beschweren und gegen irgendwas zu sein, nähern wir uns Zeiten, in denen wir wirklich etwas gestalten können.


Wir sollten sowohl in struktureller als auch in philosophischer Hinsicht auf eine freiere, egalitärere, autonomere, auf Konsens basierende Gesellschaft hinarbeiten, oder zumindest die diesen Idealen nahekommt. Ich hoffe, wir können unsere Ziele erreichen und gestärkt aus dieser Zeit des Umbruchs hervorgehen; im Idealfall könnten wir, die wir physisch und psychisch überlebt haben, sogar zu den Gründer*innen dieser neuen Gesellschaft gehören.


Leider glaube ich aber auch nicht, dass wir das so einfach schaffen werden – weder die Machthaber*innen des alten Systems noch die Rechten, die ihre Macht ausbauen wollen, werden alles tun, um einen linken Wandel oder eine Revolution zu verhindern, und sie werden die Gewalt noch deutlich weiter eskalieren lassen. Trotzdem bin ich voller Vertrauen und glaube fest daran, dass wir es schaffen werden.

author: Anonym
title: Do you remember 17. Oktober?
content:
Überlegungen und Vorschläge für die Bewegung


Die Blockaden an den Gymnasien gehen weiter, trotz der Propaganda der Regierung über das „Nachlassen der Bewegung“, mit der sie zur Resignation drängen will. In der Woche nach den Herbstferien wurden Dutzende von Oberstufenschulen blockiert, und das trotz der geänderten repressiven Politik, die darauf abzielt, die Blockaden um jeden Preis aufzuheben, die Schüler einzuschüchtern und trotz der Manipulationen der Schulbehörden, die erklären, dass eine Schule nicht als blockiert gilt, sobald sich 15 Schüler darin befinden. Die Praktiken, die seit September die Radikalität der Schülerkämpfe geprägt haben, sind nicht verschwunden. Wie schon vor den Herbstferien, die alles hätten zum Erliegen bringen können, brannten Eingangstore, wurden Feuerwerkskörper innerhalb der Schulen selbst gezündet, Schulleiter angegriffen und Schulen in Brand gesetzt, wie in Toulouse oder Lyon. Blickt man jedoch über die Tore der Oberstufenschulen hinaus, so ist seit dem 17. Oktober wenig passiert – oder vielmehr könnte das, was geschieht, leider einen langsamen Tod des aktuellen Kampfes ankündigen, der von den Gewerkschaften beschlossen sein würde, die sich mit den wenigen vom Staat gewährten Zugeständnissen zufrieden geben, wobei sich alle darauf einigen, die Konfliktlage zu entschärfen und die Revolte in den Wahlkampf von 2027 zu „übertragen“ (das heißt, nach Hause zu gehen und zur tödlichen Normalität von früher zurückzukehren).


Der 17. Oktober war Anlass für eine gewaltige Eskalation der Revolte und ermöglichte eine gewisse Ausweitung des Kampfes auf die Frage des Alltagslebens unter kapitalistischer Herrschaft, die sich wie folgt zusammenfassen ließe: immer mehr Ausbeutung, immer mehr Autorität, immer weniger Kohle zum Leben. Dieser Tag bedeutete das Eintreten zahlreicher Menschen in das Kampfgeschehen, was den von den Schülern initiierten Kämpfen eine neue Dimension verlieh, und zeugte von einem erheblichen Durchbrechen der äußeren (Ordnungskräfte) und inneren (Gewerkschaften, Parteien, demokratische Friedensstifter) Rahmenbedingungen. Seitdem ist es an den Tagen der Mobilisierungen schwierig, die zerstörerische Energie des 17. wiederzufinden, die sich damals unkontrolliert auf die Straßen ergossen hatte. Der 24. und der 31. gaben dem Staat Gelegenheit, seine Muskeln spielen zu lassen, und der Linken Gelegenheit, die Kontrolle über die Bewegung insgesamt wiederzuerlangen, indem sie alle zur Ruhe und Disziplin aufforderte. Der 5. und der 7. November verliefen nicht anders. Abgesehen von einigen Zusammenstößen und einigen Barrikaden, die nicht wirklich über das Übliche hinausgingen, verliefen die Demonstrationen überall in Frankreich geordnet oder wurden fast vollständig unterbunden. Es scheint, als sei der 17. Oktober ein Wendepunkt im Umgang mit der Aufrechterhaltung der öffentlichen Ordnung gewesen. Nachdem der Staat zunächst versucht hatte, die Bewegung durch behördliche Schließungen von Gymnasien und Hochschulen sowie zerstreute Demonstrationen langsam im Sande verlaufen zu lassen, hat er sich seit diesem Datum für rohe Gewalt entschieden und geht nun rundum repressiv vor. Zusätzlich zu den äußerst harten strafrechtlichen Maßnahmen werden zahlreiche Polizisten vor die Gymnasien geschickt, um Blockaden um jeden Preis aufzulösen und die Demonstranten einzuschüchtern; studentische Besetzungen werden sehr schnell geräumt, und die Demonstrationen dienen als Machtdemonstration mit massenhaften Festnahmen und Prügelaktionen. Das Ziel ist klar, es ist immer dasselbe: allen Angst einzujagen, ein Gefühl der Ohnmacht zu erzeugen und alle nach Hause zu treiben. Aber es ist klar, dass diese Verschleierungstaktiken, die an die Coué-Methode grenzen („nur noch 20 blockierte Gymnasien im gesamten Staatsgebiet“, obwohl jeder von uns bereits etwa zwanzig kennt), nur kurzfristig wirken und eine sofortige Wirkung auf die Rückkehr zur Normalität haben müssen, sonst fällt es auf. Die Dynamik der Schülerbewegung kann diese Taktiken leicht zunichte machen … doch dafür muss sie Bestand haben und an Stärke gewinnen.


Außerhalb der Gymnasien spielt sich der Großteil der Mobilisierung heute bei Gewerkschaftsdemonstrationen ab, seitdem die Bewegung auf das reduziert wurde, was man klassischerweise von linksorientierten sozialen Bewegungen kennt. Diese Demonstrationen, die in festgelegten Abständen stattfinden, werden von der Polizei streng überwacht und wirksam kontrolliert. Aufrufe in den sozialen Netzwerken, sich …

'yê qeyûm hatiye tayînkirin.


Nivîskarê rojnameyê Îsmail Saymaz di daxuyaniya xwe ya li ser hesabê xwe yê medyaya civakî de ev tişt gotin: 


"Polîs hatin avahiya televizyonê, li hundir lêgerîn tê kirin. Seroka Desteya Rêveber Funda Tuncer Sidali desteser kirin. Hat ragihandin ku TMSFyê ji bo kanalê qeyûm tayîn kiriye."


Parêzerê Koma Medyayê ya Sozcuyê Ersan Barkin ê ku çavdêriya lêgerîna li kanalê dike, di daxuyaniya xwe de ev agahî dan:


 "Li ser fermana Serdozgeriya Komarê ya Stenbolê, li Koma Sozcûyê lêgerîn tê kirin. Sedema vê jî dosyeyeke kevn e ku Dadgeha Bilind berê ew betal kiribû, ti neqanûnî tê de nedîtibû û erê kiribû ku ti sûc tê de nîne. Biryara qeyûm ji bo niha tenê Sozcu TV û malpera sozcu.com.tr'yê li xwe digire."


Ji aliyê din ve qeyûm dest danî ser weşana kanalê. Bernameya nûçeyan nayê weşandin.


Ozel: Tehamula wan nemaye


Berteka destpêkê ji Serokê Giştî yê Partiya NÛ Ozgur Ozel hat. Ozel di daxuyaniya xwe ya li ser hesabê xwe yê medyaya civakî de wiha got:


"Piştî Halk TVyê niha jî li ber deriyê Sozcu TVyê polîs hene, qeyûm heye. Êdî li hember rexneya herî biçûk, bihîstina rastiyeke tenê jî tehamula wan nemaye. Hatine dorpêçkirin, di heriyê de noq bûne. Ji ber vê yekê hewl didin çi û kî ji wan nebe bifetisînin. Ji bo kursiyekê welat anîn vî halî, xwelî li serê wan be. Lê em ê ne bêdeng bimînin, ne bitirsin û ne jî teslîm bibin."


Ozel wiha berdewam kir: "Hûn ê tu carî nikaribin rê li ber bilindbûna dengê vî gelî, bihîstina serhildana wî û dengvedana hawara wî bigirin. Em ê teqez rêyekê bibînin. Heke em teslîmî van dîktatorên sexte bibin, heke em vî gelî teslîmî destên wan bikin, bila dilê me bisekine."


Dervişoglu: Dengê heqîqetê dê neyê birîn


Serokê ÎYÎ Partiyê Musavat Dervişoglu jî nerazîbûna xwe ya li dijî operasyona polîsan, li ser hesabê xwe yê medyaya civakî bi peyamekê anî ziman. Peyama Dervişoğlu wiha ye:


"Operasyona li dijî Sozcu TVyê û hewldana desteserkirina fiîlî, çi hincet jê re bê nîşandan bila bê nîşandan; derbeyeke eşkere ye ku li dijî demokrasî, hiqûq, hesta edaletê û azadiya wergirtina nûçeyan a gel hatiye kirin. Tirkiye dê biaxive û dengê heqîqetê dê neyê birîn!"


(HA/AY)

author: Repórteres do projeto “Inside Deutsche Bank”
title: Inside Deutsche Bank: vazamento expõe segredos e escândalos do banco alemão
content:
O

Inside Deutsche Bank

 é uma investigação internacional baseada em 15 milhões de documentos vazados que expõem falhas do banco alemão no combate à lavagem de dinheiro e o favorecimento de clientes poderosos. O projeto reúne 230 jornalistas de mais de 50 veículos, com participação da Agência Pública, única representante do Brasil.


Mais de 15 milhões de arquivos internos. E-mails de altos executivos. Avaliações de risco confidenciais. Relatórios de transações suspeitas. Informações privadas sobre bilionários, oligarcas, políticos e membros da realeza. Registros envolvendo Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein e outros empresários sancionados. Empresas até então desconhecidas, ligadas a regimes autoritários.


Juntos, esses documentos formam o maior conjunto de arquivos internos de um banco já vazado para jornalistas.


Durante meses, mais de 200 jornalistas de todo o mundo examinaram esse vasto acervo no projeto

Inside Deutsche Bank

. Os registros abrangem algumas das atividades e funções mais sensíveis do banco: combate a crimes financeiros, monitoramento de sanções, auditorias internas e unidades responsáveis por decidir se clientes considerados de alto risco devem continuar ou não na instituição.


Quando Christian Sewing assumiu o cargo de CEO do Deutsche Bank, em 2018, após uma série de escândalos que abalou a reputação da instituição, ele prometeu que o banco seria diferente: mais estável e “um pouco mais entediante”.


Desde então, o banco vem tentando convencer o mundo de que sua era de escândalos ficou para trás.

O projeto

Inside Deutsche Bank

 coloca essa narrativa à prova

, expondo uma instituição que construiu uma enorme estrutura de

compliance

, mas que repetidamente teve dificuldades para fazê-la funcionar.


O vazamento, fornecido por duas pessoas que denunciaram irregularidades (

whistleblowers,

 no termo em inglês), foi compartilhado com o jornalista indiano Josy Joseph e a jornalista sul-africana Khadija Sharife. A Barracuda Media, uma organização sem fins lucrativos criada para analisar os dados, distribuiu o material a jornalistas de mais de 50 veículos de comunicação em mais de 60 países. A

Agência Pública

 é a única participante do Brasil. 


Os denunciantes, cujas identidades serão preservadas no projeto, copiaram os arquivos e os retiraram da instituição. Além de entregá-los a Joseph e Sharife, também forneceram material ao Departamento de Justiça dos Estados Unidos e à Rede de Combate a Crimes Financeiros do país (Financial Crimes Enforcement Network – FinCEN), conforme confirmou seu advogado.


Os arquivos mostram que diversas vezes o Deutsche Bank deixou passar sinais de alerta sobre possíveis casos de lavagem de dinheiro e violações de sanções. O banco flexibilizou suas próprias regras para atender a clientes poderosos e permitiu que interesses comerciais se sobrepusessem ao seu próprio sistema de

compliance

. Em alguns casos, a instituição só identificou falhas graves anos depois do dinheiro suspeito ter passado por seus sistemas.


Os documentos também expõem informações financeiras privadas de pessoas extremamente poderosas.


O Deutsche Bank aceitou Jeffrey Epstein como cliente em 2013, anos depois de sua condenação por aliciar uma menor para prostituição.

 O vazamento mostra que, posteriormente, o banco identificou quase US$ 600 milhões em transações suspeitas envolvendo Epstein e sua rede, mais que o dobro do valor conhecido publicamente até então.


Além de Trump e Epstein, que notoriamente recorreram ao Deutsche Bank depois que outras instituições financeiras se afastaram deles, o vazamento contém informações detalhadas sobre oligarcas aliados do presidente russo Vladimir Putin, como Oleg Deripaska e Roman Abramovich.


Entre os clientes do Deutsche Bank estava uma empresa cujo beneficiário final era um empresário saudita citado na lista “Golden Chain”, que reúne supostos financiadores da Al-Qaeda. Na condição de correspondente bancário de terceiros — quando um banco presta serviços financeiros em nome de outro — o Deutsche Bank também ajudou a processar pagamentos ligados ao falecido Rifaat al-Assad, ex-vice-presidente da Síria conhecido como “Açougueiro de Hama” por seu papel na violenta repressão de 1982 na cidade síria.


Sobre os pagamentos relacionados a al-Assad, o Deutsche Bank declarou:


“Este caso foi encerrado em 2022, conforme divulgado publicamente. No âmbito da investigação conduzida pelo Ministério Público de Frankfurt em relação a dois relatórios de …

author: Rafael Oliveira
title: “Picaretas não melhoram”, disse executivo do Deutsche Bank sobre André Esteves, do BTG
content:
O

Inside Deutsche Bank

 é uma investigação internacional baseada em 15 milhões de documentos vazados que expõem falhas do banco alemão no combate à lavagem de dinheiro e o favorecimento de clientes poderosos. O projeto reúne 230 jornalistas de mais de 50 veículos, com participação da Agência Pública, única representante do Brasil.


“Se tem uma coisa que a experiência me ensinou, é que picaretas não melhoram milagrosamente com a idade. Eles podem até ganhar uma aparência de respeitabilidade, mas, quando a coisa aperta, o picareta que está por trás acaba reaparecendo”.


À primeira vista, quem lê o parágrafo acima pode imaginar se tratar de algum roteiro de filme de baixo orçamento, ou talvez um trecho de uma novela pastelão. Não é o caso.


A frase em questão foi escrita por John MacNamara em um email de outubro de 2018, quando ele era o Chefe Global de Commodities do Deutsche Bank (DB), um dos maiores bancos do mundo, presente no Brasil há mais de um século. MacNamara, um executivo de peso que trabalhou no banco durante duas décadas, se referia a André Esteves, o acionista controlador de um dos principais clientes da instituição alemã na América Latina, o BTG Pactual, maior banco de investimentos do continente. 


Na época da mensagem, Esteves já figurava entre os mais ricos do Brasil. Segundo a

lista

 da Forbes de 2026, ele agora acumula uma fortuna superior a R$ 100 bilhões, a terceira maior do país.


A crítica ao banqueiro está presente em uma troca de emails internos do banco alemão sobre uma negociação que envolvia BTG e Petrobras analisada pela

Agência Pública

. 


O material é parte do

Inside Deutsche Bank

, investigação transnacional da qual a

Pública

 faz parte, baseada no vazamento de mais de 15 milhões de documentos do banco, obtido pelos jornalistas sul-africanos Josy Joseph e Khadija Sharife. O projeto tem coordenação global da Barracuda Media e do Centro Latinoamericano de Periodismo de Investigación (CLIP) na região.


Os documentos vazados para o projeto mostram,

segundo detalhado em diversas reportagens

, como o banco alemão repetidamente ignorou sinais de alerta de possível lavagem de dinheiro e violações de sanções e como descumpriu suas próprias regras para clientes poderosos.


Em entrevista à

Pública

, MacNamara afirmou que sua recusa em trabalhar com o BTG Pactual e André Esteves na época teve a ver com o que chama de “solução mágica” do banqueiro brasileiro em caso que envolve a trading Sementes Selecta (atualmente conhecida como CJ Selecta). A empresa enfrentou recuperação judicial a partir de 2008 e, naquele período, deixou de pagar dívidas. O Deutsche Bank era um dos credores da Selecta.


Segundo o relato de MacNamara, depois de os credores passarem anos tentando recuperar os recursos em tribunais brasileiros, sem sucesso, André Esteves teria aparecido  “com uma solução mágica, trazendo dinheiro novo, que protegeu o capital dos acionistas originais” e tornou o banco brasileiro acionista “de graça”, enquanto os bancos a quem a Selecta devia tiveram de aceitar o prejuízo. 


“Nunca vi uma reestruturação em que os detentores de capital tivessem prioridade sobre os detentores de dívida. Tivemos várias reuniões; eles nos ofereceram um acordo privado para apoiar o plano, mas recusamos.

 Esse tipo de risco reputacional era algo de que podíamos prescindir. Depois disso, me recusei a voltar a fazer negócios com eles”, explica o executivo do setor de

commodities

, que diz que Esteves “não tinha a bússola moral correta”. 


Tempos depois do episódio, ele conta, chegou a receber uma proposta de emprego do banco brasileiro, quando o BTG ampliou sua atuação na Europa. “Talvez para me calar? Quem sabe…”, diz.


André Esteves e o BTG foram procurados pela reportagem por meio de sua assessoria de imprensa com

perguntas detalhadas

, mas preferiram não se pronunciar oficialmente.


Apesar de MacNamara alegar ter motivos para se recusar a trabalhar com Esteves e o BTG Pactual,

outros emails internos do Deutsche Bank revisados pela reportagem

demonstram que executivos do banco que trabalhavam dentro e fora do Brasil defenderam veementemente a relação com Esteves

, o que revela

visões contrastantes dentro do próprio banco alemão.

 Em um deles, um funcionário afirmou que a posição de Mac “claramente não reflete a visão institucional do Deutsche Bank”. Nos anos seguintes, a executiva que substituiu MacNamara tentou retomar o negócio.

author: Aaron Ernest Cruz
title: ‘Unconstitutional’ — lawyers on checkpoints blocking, delaying protesters
content:
Southern Tagalog delegates negotiating with the police who block their way going to Liwasang Bonifacio. Photo from UPLB Perspective

“These rights have primacy in all constitutional rights. This is the highest constitutional right that the government should protect at all cost.”

As police continue to block protesters from different places using checkpoints, progressive lawyers said the police are interrupting not only the rights of the people to protest but also of Filipinos who are working during the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Delegates from Southern Tagalog who held the Lakbayan ng Timog Katalugan (Southern Tagalog caravan) starting on November 12, faced police brutality during their march to Liwasang Bonifacio.

Previously, they have been repeatedly blocked by police forces. Reports from UPLB Perspective shows punctured tires from the vehicles used by the delegates. The harassment continued where police disrupted the delegates when they barricaded the road at midnight to prevent them from moving forward.

On November 15, police brutality took over as they violently arrested almost 270 delegates while holding a peaceful mobilization. As of this writing, the National Union of People’s Lawyers and Koalisyong Makabayan have gained access to those arrested.

In the University of the Philippines, hundreds of police were deployed to man checkpoints at the exit points. The PICC and nearby areas were also heavily guarded. Aside from these checkpoints, there are also other checkpoints conducted in the borders of several provinces and the National Capital Region.

In an interview, National Union of Peoples’ Lawyer (NUPL) Ephraim “Rey” Cortez underscores that mass deployment of checkpoints within the area violates freedom of expression and right to peaceful assembly that is protected under the Philippine constitution.

“These rights have primacy in all constitutional rights. This is the highest constitutional right that the government should protect at all cost,” Cortez asserted.

Cortez also explained that freedom of expression should include the right of people to protest not just in any designated freedom park such as the Liwasang Bonifacio but anywhere without needing to secure a permit.

In Batas Pambansa Bldg. 880, going to freedom park to protest does not need a permit or any travel pass. Lawyers like the NUPL argue that blocking protesters while officials cannot identify clear and present danger is unconstitutional.

The said law has been facing criticism by NUPL stating that “this dictatorship-era law that places constitutional rights of the people to collective action under a system of prior state approval.”

Aside from rally permit arguments, Cortez added that traffic regulations should not also be used as a tool to suppress or stop the people going to freedom park where they can protest to amplify their call against police brutality and opposition to Pax Silica where thousands of Ayta and local farmers will lose their livelihood.

“As long as there is no clear and present danger, [it] cannot prevail over the exercise of constitutional guaranteed rights,” Cortez explained.

As there are no specific laws on checkpoints, the Supreme Court has previous decisions such as the Valmonte vs. De Villa, which states that checkpoint is not illegal but law enforcement shall be limited to visual search.

In Aniag Jr. vs COMELEC, it is stated that police should only have access to a vehicle if they have probable cause or voluntary consent. None of the ruling states that checkpoints can be used to block protesters, especially going to freedom park.

“You are conducting a checkpoint because there is an impending criminal act to be committed. But if the checkpoint is used because of protest, it violates their constitutional rights […] You can’t put the blame on protesters as they are continuously moving and exercising their rights,” Cortez said.

According to Cortez, it is not the people who participated in the rally causing traffic, the blame should fall on the police who continuously block the protesters’ way to raise their legitimate concerns.

As police brutality continues, progressive groups vow to push through with their protests to amplify the call of the marginalized groups especially to Indigenous and local communities who will be affected once the Pax Silica is officially constructed. (AMU, RVO)

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Groups condemn police brutality, state repression against anti-Pax Silica protesters
content:
Police officers arrest a protester during a protest in Liwasang Bonifacio on November 15, 2026. Photo by Adrian Puse/Altermidya

MANILA — “Trump was given a red carpet but the Filipino people are given fascism and repression, and are prevented from expressing their opposition to Pax Silica.”

This is the statement of Dr. Ganni Tapang, leaf convener of the Network Opposed to Pax Silica.

Representatives of different progressive groups condemned the state’s attacks against Filipino activists, journalists, and Indigenous people in a press conference at Vinzon’s compound at the University of the Philippines–Diliman.

Around 500 personnel of the Philippine National Police (PNP) were spotted surrounding the perimeter of campus. They were stationed around the entrance and exits of campus, along Katipunan Avenue, University Avenue, and College of Science among others.

Tapang, also the former Dean of the College of Science, condemned the collusion of the Philippine government with the US, specifically Marcos Jr.’s enabling the Pax Silica Initiative to plunder the country.

“The PNP should be defending our rights and not curtailing them, and following the orders of Donald Trump and President Marcos,” Tapang said.

The Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica launched on campus on Friday, November 13, and will continue until November 16. This was participated by 200 Ayta, including 50 from Cordillera, 500 farmers and youth from Central Luzon, and many volunteers and community members.

Although UP is a sanctuary campus, student journalists from the College of Mass Communication covering the protests suffered from attempted arrests.

Dr. Ma. Diosa Labiste, dean of the UP College of Media and Communications, said that this is the police’s attempt to prevent legitimate dissent in the course of the ASEAN summit.

“We demand the police to recognize the citizens to participate in protest actions,” said Labiste. “We will hold the police accountable if our students are harmed when they are doing their job as campus journalists.”

“Journalism is not illegal,” said Yvo Asis, multimedia editor of the Philippine Collegian. He shared about a student journalist from UP who was arrested in Sucat, Muntinlupa while on the ground.

The police did not read to them the Miranda rights and later on brought a truck full of people to Camp Bagong Diwa. Over 300 were arrested, with the largest contingent coming from Southern Tagalog.

“It is the democratic right of the Filipino masses to spread the developments of Pax Silica.” Paul Viuya, Chairperson of BAYAN Central Luzon, said that these arrests expose the true face of fascism in our country.

Of those arrested, twelve were injured, including someone who fainted and was still kicked in the head by the police, according to Teacher Kat Ortega, president of the All UP Academic Employees Union.

Ortega also condemned the arrest of three students of the University of Makati while participating in the November 13 nationwide student walkout. “They are not criminals. They are just peacefully expressing their indignation,” she said.

Activists in Liwasang Bonifacio shared to Ortega how the police scattered human feces and urine around Freedom Park on November 15. They also took the rallyists’ belongings, and slashed the tires of the activists’ trucks while they were setting up for the protest.

The Philippine government allotted P22.9 billion (US$358 million) for hosting the ASEAN Summit.. Ortega said that these could have been used for social services and building classrooms that serve the Filipino people. Instead, it is used for the advancement of Pax Silica, which will take the country’s water, electricity, and labor power.

“We call on the PNP. Arrest Atong Ang, Zaldy Co, Bato dela Rosa, and all of the corrupt politicians. Block Donald Trump, who wages war against the people of the world,” said Ortega. “They are the true criminals who destroy peoples’ lives.”

Amid repression, Erich Jones Escototo, convener of UP Against Pax Silica (UPAX) said that nothing could silence the voices of the oppressed Filipino masses.

“The Filipino people continue to resist.” Escototo called on fellow students to join the protests in Liwasang Bonifacio on November 17 where different sectors from all over the country will express their indignation.

“What the masses want is the freedom to protest,” said Tapang, calling on the Filipino people to stand for their right to protest and to convey their demands and opposition. (RVO)

author: Kodao Productions
title: By suppressing Pax Silica foes, gov’t lost
content:
The Marcos Jr. administration should stop acting with unctuous servility to Donald Trump by whitewashing the metropolis, putting up Potemkin villages where the ragged people live and sabotaging protest actions against Pax Silica by destroying the brakes of vehicles used by the Lakbayan marchers, mauling three students of the University of Makati, rounding up 278 workers, farmers and activists in Muntinlupa, Paranaque, arresting nine protesters in Laguna, stopping DLTB buses from plying the UP Los Banos-UP Diliman route out of fear that they would ferry protesters to Metro Manila, preventing a delegation from Bulacan to enter the metropolis and nabbing 21 activists at Liwasang Bonifacio.


Why do we have to engage in *scurryfunge and give Trump a tongue bath when he was resoundingly repudiated by the US electorate in the midterm elections by giving to the Democrats 28 statehouses, 56 seats at the Senate and majority of the House of Representatives, with the margin at 140, the worst beating suffered by addled Republican politicians in history.


For the edification of the foremost defenders of Pax Silica and the data centers that it requires, US voters rejected data centers, with potential $68-billion investment going up in smoke in many states. If this Pax Silica castle in the air were a cornucopia of investment that would eliminate poverty (and about 29% of Americans are now dirt-poor), create millions of jobs and usher in a Golden Era facilitated by Trump, why did hundreds of millions of US voters junk it? Pax Silica may well be phantasmagoria.


Malacanang has broken the record for mass arrests by suppressing the right of the Filipino people to organize, protest and seek redress of grievances as guaranteed by the 1987 Constitution. There is no legal justification at all for suppressing civil and political liberties just to please the lawless Trump, who has inflicted the worst economic burden on humanity when he, at the instigation of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a war against Iran and caused oil and gas prices to skyrocket. Trump, who barely reads, only operates to line his pockets and those of his tech pals led by Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Peter Thiel, Jensen Huang and other billionaires who have secured subsidies, tax breaks and favorable policies from Trump, who has enriched himself to the tune of $5-billion in his unlamented return to the White House.


Government has mobilized thousands of policemen and soldiers to secure the venue of the ASEAN Summit and the hotels housing delegates to the summit in a vain attempt to show that Filipinos will not protest the opaque Pax Silica Initiative that many insist was

author: Victoria Python
title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
content:
The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches.


Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred.


While the White House and leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate

new

 protocols are largely unnecessary. Following

existing

 best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems.


Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code.


Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. To the extent that gaps in existing laws warrant new legislation, EFF recommends the following policy framework:


STATUTORY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS:

Lawmakers should enact legislation that requires AI developers to adhere to well-established cybersecurity best practices when testing AI systems, such as strong sandboxing and network isolation, least-privilege access, effective logging and monitoring, and clear incident-response procedures


REGULATORY STANDARDS:

Congress should require an existing federal agency, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

1

, to adopt safety standards for pre-deployment development and testing of generative AI systems, based on the established best practices referenced above. The agency should be required to update the standards every 2 years, or earlier as needed due to reported security incidents and/or major technological advancements. These standards should be developed in consultation with academic and nonprofit AI researchers, civil liberties organizations, and commercial AI developers, and adopted through formal agency rulemaking following a notice and comment process. That consultation should include an assessment of potential adverse impacts on competition, with the goal of ensuring that regulatory standards do not effectively lock out potential competitors.


LIABILITY:

The law should provide for civil liability for AI development and testing that results in unauthorized access to a third party system, if performed under conditions that do not satisfy cybersecurity standards adopted by NIST, or another federal agency responsible for adopting these regulations, unless the company proves it acted reasonably under the circumstances to prevent unauthorized access to third party system 


ENFORCEMENT:

Both federal and state authorities should be able to hold AI developers accountable where they have failed to meet the minimum standards adopted by the designated federal agency, such as NIST. author: CMI Argentina
title: Santa Fe: el río Paraná superó el nivel de evacuación
content:
El crecimiento del nivel del agua en Santa Fe genera preocupación en distintas localidades y barrios de la zona. Desde el jueves pasado, la crecida avanza a un ritmo de aproximadamente 15 centímetros por día y ya obligó a evacuar familias en Arroyo Leyes, ubicada a 23 kilómetros de la capital provincial.


Escuchar el reporte de Radio Chalet de Santa Fe


“Estamos complicados y evacuando a las familias”, advirtió Eduardo Lorinz, presidente comunal de Arroyo Leyes, quien explicó que hasta el jueves la situación se mantenía tranquila, pero que desde entonces el ingreso de agua se aceleró.


“Nos tuvo todo el fin de semana ocupado, realmente, un poco las corridas, porque, a diferencia de otras emergencias, esta fue muy rápida”, relató.


El funcionario también manifestó su preocupación por la situación de uno de los barrios de la localidad, que habitualmente resiste las crecidas, pero que esta vez se encuentra “bastante colapsado”.


La situación también es compleja en Alto Verde, otro de los sectores de la ciudad de Santa Fe históricamente afectados por las inundaciones. Luis Alba, presidente de la vecinal del barrio, informó que el domingo pasado quedó cortado el camino que constituye la única vía de ingreso a ese sector.


Alba advirtió además sobre el riesgo que implicaría una eventual rotura de la defensa ubicada del lado del canal de acceso. Según explicó, si eso ocurriera, entre el 80 y el 90 por ciento de Alto Verde podría quedar bajo el agua, con niveles de entre un metro y medio y dos metros dentro de las viviendas.


El vecinalista señaló que el barrio no cuenta con maquinaria propia para responder ante una emergencia de esas características y alertó sobre el tiempo que demandaría la llegada de equipos, camiones y materiales para contener una posible rotura.

https://agencia.farco.org.ar/2026/11/16/santa-fe-el-rio-parana-supero-el-nivel-de-evacuacion/

author: Cierra Bettens
title: InFocus: Is adopting permanent daylight saving time a mistake?
content:
Many of us know how we feel when it’s time to change our clocks back in the fall and forward in the spring. Sleepy – maybe even a little disoriented.

Well, on Nov. 1, citizens in six provinces and territories didn’t experience any of that because their governments scrapped the dreaded seasonal time change.

Governments had two choices: stick with standard time or daylight saving time. Standard time gives you more sun in the morning – while daylight time gives you extended sun in the evening.

Most chose to extend daylight into the evening.

But will they regret their decision?

This week on InFocus, David Prerau, one of the world’s foremost experts on daylight saving time, explains why they might.

“What happened in the U.S. anyway is nobody was much against it until it actually occurred in January 1974,” Prerau, the author of Seize the Daylight, told host Cierra Bettens. “We had an incident in 1974 where there was an energy crisis, an unexpected energy crisis. And so they put in daylight saving time year-round for a two-year period, which they thought would cover the energy crisis. And most people thought it would be good until it happened.

“Everybody saw they had to get up in the pitch dark, go to work in the pitch dark, and most people thought the worst thing was that to send their kids to school in the dark, walking on dark city streets or waiting at the bus stop on dark country roads. And so it lost popularity very quickly in the US, and I think 1974 and even though it was only a two-year plan, they got rid of it after one year because it was so unpopular.”

Anishinaabe health scholar, Dr. Amy Shawanda, said if the government wants to adopt one particular time, she supports standard time. But she added, there are impacts of changing the clocks.

“It’s not natural to our circadian rhythms,” she said. “A lot of people will feel off when the clocks change because it’s not natural to our circadian rhythms. As Indigenous Peoples, we never had to change the clocks. We just lived on the land, and so it’s not natural to who we are.

“We should really move away from the daylight saving time and not adopt it at all, because it does really go against our own circadian rhythms. It goes against our biology.”

Cierra is the host and co-producer of the of the weekly APTN News InFocus podcast. She joined APTN in 2024 as a reporter-correspondent in Winnipeg after working in campus and city news. She’s currently completing her Master of Arts in Media Studies at Concordia University in Montréal. Cierra has mixed settler and Red River Métis roots and is a member of the Manitoba Métis Federation.
